title: Symmetry in nature and art: moves that change nothing, and how nature breaks them

summary.text: A square card fits back into its own outline in eight different ways, but a plain triangle cut at random fits in only one. Count the ways, and a shape's symmetry becomes a number. Your child counts the fits, builds border patterns from five moves, and finds that a left hand cannot be turned into a right hand. Then a straight strip, pushed equally from both ends, bends to one side anyway. Nature uses this to give a body a left and a right, and physics uses it to explain why energy is never lost. A chemistry puzzle remains open: life uses only left-handed building blocks, and nobody knows why.
summary.art: A square card sitting inside its outline on a table, with a straight card strip bowed to one side beside it and a left hand and a right hand placed palm to palm.

intro.hook: Hold up your left hand, then your right. They are the same size, with the same fingers in the same order. Now try to lay your left hand exactly on top of your right, both palms down. You cannot, however you turn it. What is different between two things that match in every measurement?
intro.text: In Class 3 you found lines of symmetry by folding and rotational symmetry by turning. Now we go one step deeper. A symmetry is any move that leaves a shape looking the same. You will count all the moves a shape allows, see why borders on sarees come in exactly seven kinds, and find out why hands, screws and shells have a handedness. Then you will push a strip and watch a perfectly even push make a lopsided bend.
intro.art: A left hand and a right hand drawn as paper cut-outs, one laid over the other, with the thumbs pointing in opposite directions.

outcomes: I can name four moves that can leave a shape looking the same: a flip, a turn, a slide and a glide.
I can count every way a shape fits back into its own outline, and explain why a regular shape with n sides fits back in 2 times n ways.
I can make border patterns with a stencil and say how many kinds of border pattern exist.
I can explain why a left hand cannot be turned to fit a right hand, and name three things in nature or at home that have a handedness.
I can explain symmetry breaking using the pushed strip: an even push, a lopsided bend, and a tiny difference that decides the direction.
I can give two ways that a lopsided body part helps a living being, and say what is still not known about how a body gets its left and right.
I can say in simple words what Emmy Noether and Chien-Shiung Wu each found about symmetry in the laws of nature.

terms.meaning: A move that leaves a shape looking exactly the same as before. The move can be a flip, a turn, a slide or a glide.
terms.example: A steel thali looks the same after any turn. So turning is a symmetry of the thali.
terms.art: A round steel thali with a small curved arrow showing it being turned, and an identical thali beside it.

terms.meaning: A flip over a line, like looking in a mirror. Every point goes to the same distance on the other side of the line.
terms.example: A butterfly's left wing is the reflection of the right wing.
terms.art: A butterfly seen from above with a dotted line down the middle and matching wings on each side.

terms.meaning: A turn of a shape around a fixed point called the centre.
terms.example: A ceiling fan with three blades looks the same after one third of a turn.
terms.art: A three-bladed ceiling fan seen from below with a curved arrow showing a one third turn.

terms.meaning: A slide of a shape in a straight line without turning or flipping it.
terms.example: The same flower is printed again and again along a border, each one slid a little to the right.
terms.art: A row of identical flowers along a saree border, with an arrow showing each flower slid to the right.

terms.meaning: A flip and a slide done together. The shape is flipped over a line and slid along the line.
terms.example: Footprints in wet sand: the left footprint and the right footprint glide along the path.
terms.art: Footprints on sand, left and right, alternating along a straight path with a dotted line down the middle.

terms.meaning: The do-nothing move. Every shape fits back onto itself if you leave it where it is, so the identity always counts as one symmetry.
terms.example: Even the letter F, which has no flip or turn that works, has the identity.
terms.art: The letter F sitting still inside its own outline with a tick beside it.

terms.meaning: What you see in a flat mirror. It looks like the thing, but with left and right reversed.
terms.example: The mirror image of your right hand looks like a left hand.
terms.art: A right hand held up to a mirror, with a left hand looking back.

terms.meaning: A thing is handed if its mirror image cannot be turned to match it. Scientists also say the thing is chiral, from the Greek word for hand.
terms.example: A glove is handed. A steel katori is not, because it matches its mirror image.
terms.art: A pair of gloves, one left and one right, and a steel katori beside them.

terms.meaning: A shape that winds round like a spring or a screw thread. A helix can wind one way or the other.
terms.example: The thread on a jar lid is a helix. So is the shape of DNA.
terms.art: A coiled spring drawn from the side, with a thin arrow following the coil upwards.

terms.meaning: A pattern that repeats along a line, like the border of a saree or a band of carving on a temple wall. Mathematicians call it a frieze pattern.
terms.example: The row of small temples painted along the edge of a Kanchipuram saree is a border pattern.
terms.art: A saree border with a row of small temple shapes repeating along it.

terms.meaning: A pattern that covers a flat surface completely with repeating shapes, with no gaps and no overlaps.
terms.example: A bathroom floor of square tiles is a tiling. So is a honeycomb.
terms.art: A floor covered in square and octagonal tiles in two colours.

terms.meaning: When something that starts out perfectly even ends up lopsided. A tiny difference decides which way it goes.
terms.example: A tall pencil balanced on its tip must fall, and it falls one way, though nothing pushed it.
terms.art: A pencil standing on its tip and the same pencil lying on the table, with a curved arrow between them.

terms.meaning: To bend suddenly sideways when pushed hard from the ends.
terms.example: A thin plastic ruler buckles when you push its two ends towards each other.
terms.art: A plastic ruler held at both ends by two hands and bowed into a curve.

terms.meaning: A living being at the very beginning of growth, before the body has taken shape.
terms.example: A chick embryo inside an egg, in the first days, is a tiny curled body.
terms.art: A tiny curled chick embryo shown inside a cut-open egg.

terms.meaning: A solid whose tiny particles are arranged in a pattern that repeats in every direction.
terms.example: A grain of salt is a tiny cube-shaped crystal.
terms.art: A grain of salt magnified, showing a neat cube.

terms.meaning: A solid with an orderly pattern of particles that never exactly repeats. The word means 'almost a crystal'.
terms.example: Some quasicrystals have a five-fold symmetry, which an ordinary crystal can never have.
terms.art: A pattern of two kinds of rhombus tiles making a star with five points that never repeats.

terms.meaning: Kept the same total, never made or lost. Scientists say energy is conserved, because it can move or change form but the total stays the same.
terms.example: A swinging swing slows down and stops. Its energy has gone into warming the air and the rope, not vanished.
terms.art: A swing at the top of its swing and again at rest, with arrows showing energy moving into warm air.

terms.meaning: A tiny living being, far smaller than a bacterium, that lives inside the cells of other living beings. Many viruses build a shell from many identical pieces.
terms.example: Many viruses have a shell with 20 flat triangular faces.
terms.art: A magnified virus drawn as a ball with 20 triangular faces.

terms.meaning: Tiny hairs on the surface of a cell that wave or spin. Cilia can push fluid along.
terms.example: The cilia in your windpipe sweep dust and mucus upwards.
terms.art: A cell with many tiny hairs along its surface, all bent the same way.

explanations.concept: Symmetry is a move that changes nothing
explanations.definition: A symmetry of a shape is a move, such as a flip, a turn, a slide or a glide, after which the shape looks exactly as it did before.
explanations.description: In Class 3 you tested for a fold line and for a turn. Those are two of four moves. A flip swaps the two sides of a line. A turn spins the shape round a centre. A slide moves it along without turning it. A glide flips it and slides it at the same time. A single shape, such as the outline of a butterfly, can only be flipped or turned back onto its own outline. But a pattern that goes on and on, such as a saree border, can be slid and glided onto itself as well. A move counts as a symmetry only if every part lands on a matching part. Mathematicians describe a shape or a pattern by listing all its symmetries.
examples: A steel thali: any turn, and a flip over any line through its centre.
A saree border of identical mangoes: a slide to the next mango.
Footprints along a path: a glide, because the left foot and the right foot alternate.
The letter F: only the do-nothing move.
explanations.art: Four small drawings of the letter F with arrows: flipped, turned, slid and glided.

explanations.concept: Counting every way a shape fits back
explanations.definition: The symmetry count of a shape is the number of different ways it can fit back into its own outline, counting the do-nothing move as one.
explanations.description: Cut a square from card and trace around it. Now find every way to put it back in its outline. You can leave it, turn it a quarter, a half, three quarters, and you can flip it and turn it in the same ways. That is 4 turns and 4 flips, which makes 8. An equilateral triangle, with three equal sides, fits back in 6 ways. A rectangle that is not a square fits in 4. A triangle with three different sides fits in only 1, the do-nothing move. A regular shape with n equal sides always fits back in 2 times n ways: n turns and n flips. A circle fits back in endless ways. A shape with a higher symmetry count looks more regular.
examples: Square: 8 ways.
Equilateral triangle: 6 ways.
Rectangle that is not a square: 4 ways.
Regular hexagon, like a honeycomb cell: 12 ways.
explanations.art: A square, a triangle, a rectangle and a hexagon in a row, each with its number of fits written below.

explanations.concept: Borders and floors: seven and seventeen
explanations.definition: There are exactly seven different kinds of border pattern, and exactly seventeen different kinds of pattern that cover a flat floor.
explanations.description: A border is a pattern that repeats along a line. You can build one from a single shape, such as the letter F, by repeating it with a slide, a glide, a flip over a line across the border, a flip over a line along the border, or a half turn. Mix these moves and you get exactly seven border patterns, and not an eighth. For a floor, the pattern repeats in two directions. Mathematicians showed there are exactly seventeen kinds. A Russian crystal scientist, Evgraf Fedorov, proved this in 1891, and the mathematician George Pólya found the same result again in 1924. Many designers in the world have used all kinds without knowing the count, and the count is a surprise: the possible patterns are not endless.
examples: The row of mangoes on a Kanchipuram saree border: a slide.
A border of leaves that point alternately up and down: a glide.
A row of diyas whose reflection is also a diya: a flip over a line along the border.
A tiled floor of squares or hexagons.
explanations.art: A saree border pattern, a temple carving band and a tiled floor, each with a small arrow showing how it repeats.

explanations.concept: Left and right: why a hand cannot be turned into its twin
explanations.definition: A thing is handed, or chiral, if its mirror image cannot be turned to match the original. A left hand and a right hand are mirror twins.
explanations.description: Lay a cut-out of your left hand on your right hand outline, both facing the same way up. It does not fit. Flip it over and it fits. A flat cut-out can be flipped over to fit. A real hand lives in space and cannot be flipped. It can only be turned. So a left glove will never fit your right hand, however you turn it. In a flat drawing, any shape with no line of symmetry is handed. A screw thread is handed: nearly every jar lid tightens by turning to the right. Many climbing plants twine round a pole in one direction, and most snail shells coil the same way. Handedness is not the same as being uneven. A left hand is not worse than a right hand. They are exact twins that differ only in a way that no turning can change.
examples: Gloves, shoes and left and right hands.
A jar lid or bolt: the thread winds one way.
The tusk of a narwhal almost always spirals in one direction.
The letters F, R, G and S, which cannot be flipped onto themselves by turning.
explanations.art: A left and a right hand cut-out, side by side, with the right one flipped over and now matching.

explanations.concept: Life uses one hand of many molecules
explanations.description: Many molecules come in a left-handed and a right-handed form, like gloves. Chemists can make both forms in the laboratory, in equal amounts. But the living world mostly uses just one. The amino acids that build proteins are almost all left-handed. Common sugars in living bodies are right-handed. The twist of the DNA double helix is right-handed. Nobody is sure why life ended up with one hand. This is one of the open puzzles in science.
examples: Proteins are built from left-handed amino acids.
The double helix of DNA winds to the right.
Two forms of the same molecule can smell different. One form of a molecule called carvone smells of spearmint and the other of caraway.

perspectives.explanation: Early on, a tiny random excess of one hand in some place got copied and grew until life used only that hand. It could just as easily have been the other.

Chien-Shiung Wu showed that one force inside atoms treats left and right differently. A few scientists think this nudged molecules a very little towards one hand. The effect is very small and not shown to be enough.

Some meteorites, such as the one that fell near Murchison in Australia in 1969, hold amino acids, some of them reported with a slight excess of the left-handed form. The idea is that such rocks seeded the young Earth. Whether this is the cause is not known.

explanations.art: Two molecule models that are mirror images of each other, like a pair of gloves, with one marked as used by life.

explanations.concept: Symmetry breaking: an even start, a lopsided end
explanations.definition: Symmetry breaking happens when a system that is perfectly even at the start ends up lopsided, and a tiny difference decides which way it goes.
explanations.description: Stand a pencil on its sharp tip. It cannot stay up, and it falls. Before it falls, every direction is equal. After it falls, it points in one direction. Nothing pushed it harder from one side. A tiny draught, a speck on the table or a tiny wobble in the wood decided. In the same way, a thin straight ruler pushed equally from both ends buckles to the left or to the right. A tiny bend in the ruler or a tiny difference in your fingers decides which. Once it has gone one way, the symmetry is broken. A symmetric cause can have a lopsided result. The other way round, a very small difference can make a very big change in the shape of things. Physicists think the same idea shaped the early universe. They think the early universe was almost perfectly even, and tiny differences grew into stars and galaxies.
examples: A pencil balanced on its tip falls one way.
A straight ruler buckles left or right.
A pea on top of a smooth upturned bowl rolls down one side.
A drinking straw bent by squeezing its ends goes one way or the other.
explanations.art: A pencil standing on its tip, with a ring of equal arrows pointing round it, and the pencil lying down pointing one way.

explanations.concept: How a body gets a left and a right
explanations.description: A human embryo starts as a ball of cells that looks almost the same on every side. Later the body has a left and a right. Most people have the heart on the left, the liver on the right and the stomach tilted to the left. A few people have all their organs the other way round, and they are usually healthy. How does a ball of cells choose a side? The question is not settled. In mouse embryos, a small pit has tiny spinning hairs called cilia. They all spin the same way and sweep the fluid in the pit towards one side. This flow is thought to start the difference. How a first tiny difference gets to the pit is still being studied.
examples: In most people, the heart sits to the left and the liver to the right.
In a few people, the organs are mirrored. This is rare.
In an embryo, the gut tube loops round in a set direction.

perspectives.explanation: In the mouse, spinning cilia sweep fluid to the left and start a chain of signals on that side. Many scientists think humans work in a similar way.

In some animals, such as frogs and chicks, an earlier difference may be set before the cilia start, perhaps by electrical signals between the first cells. How much this matters in humans is not known.

explanations.art: A magnified pit in an embryo with tiny spinning hairs sweeping fluid to one side, and an arrow towards the left.

explanations.concept: Asymmetry that helps a living being
explanations.definition: Many living beings are not even on purpose: a lopsided part can give them a skill that an even body could not have.
explanations.description: A flounder starts life as a baby that swims upright, with one eye on each side. As the baby grows, one eye slowly moves across the head to join the other. The adult lies on one side on the sea floor with both eyes looking up. A barn owl's ears sit at different heights on her head. A sound from above reaches one ear a tiny moment before the other, and she uses that to find a mouse she cannot see. A male fiddler crab grows one huge claw on one side, for fighting and for waving at females. Almost all narwhal tusks spiral the same way. A little unevenness is not a mistake in these cases. It is the way the body does a job.
examples: A flounder with both eyes on the same side.
An owl with ears at different heights.
A male fiddler crab waving one large claw.
The narwhal's spiral tusk.
explanations.art: A flounder lying on the sea floor with both eyes on top, next to a barn owl's face with the ears at different heights.

explanations.definition: Crystals, viruses and many small living things are built from many identical copies of one piece, and this makes them symmetrical.
explanations.description: A grain of salt is a tiny cube because its particles stack in a cubic pattern that repeats in every direction. Ice makes hexagon patterns. Many viruses build their shell out of many copies of the same protein. Each copy fits into a spot among its neighbours, and the shell ends up as a 20-sided shape with 20 triangular faces. This saves the virus effort. A virus only has to carry the instructions for one small piece, and the copies join themselves. Tiny sea creatures called radiolarians make glassy skeletons with beautiful symmetry. In every case, building from identical copies makes symmetry almost automatic.
examples: A grain of salt: a cube.
A snow crystal: six arms.
Many viruses: a shell with 20 triangular faces.
A pollen grain: often a round ball with a regular pattern of pores.
explanations.art: A grain of salt, a snowflake and a virus shell drawn side by side, each with matching parts marked.

explanations.definition: A quasicrystal is an orderly solid whose pattern of particles never exactly repeats, even though it has a regular, five-fold or ten-fold symmetry.
explanations.description: A pattern that repeats by sliding, such as wallpaper, can only have 2-fold, 3-fold, 4-fold or 6-fold symmetry. A five-fold pattern cannot fill a floor with repeating tiles. Pentagons leave gaps. In 1982, Dan Shechtman, a scientist in the United States, saw a five-fold pattern in a diffraction picture of a metal mixture. Most crystal scientists said it was impossible. The famous chemist Linus Pauling is reported to have said there were no quasicrystals, only quasi-scientists. Shechtman says he was asked to leave his research group. But the evidence held. In 2011 he won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The mathematician Roger Penrose had already drawn floor patterns with five-fold symmetry that never repeat, in the 1970s. Natural quasicrystals have since been found in a meteorite. Some medieval tilings in West Asia, such as those on a shrine in Isfahan, look like Penrose patterns.
examples: Penrose tiling: two shapes of tile make a never-repeating floor.
A metal mixture of aluminium and manganese in which Shechtman saw a five-fold pattern.
Girih tilings on old buildings in Iran and Central Asia, which some scientists say come close to quasicrystal patterns.
explanations.art: A Penrose tiling of two kinds of rhombus tile making a five-pointed star in the middle.

explanations.concept: Why the laws of nature have symmetry: Emmy Noether
explanations.definition: Noether's theorem says that every smooth symmetry in the laws of nature goes with something that is never used up. The laws do not change from one moment to the next, and that is why energy is conserved.
explanations.description: Suppose a physicist does the same experiment on Monday and on Tuesday and gets the same result. The laws of nature are the same at both times. That is a symmetry: sliding the experiment along time changes nothing. In 1918, the German mathematician Emmy Noether proved that this particular symmetry means energy can never be made or lost. A different symmetry, that the laws are the same in every place, means a thing called momentum is conserved. A third, that the laws are the same in every direction, means angular momentum, the amount of spinning, is conserved. Noether was not allowed to hold a paid university post for years because she was a woman. A famous mathematician, David Hilbert, argued for her, and she was finally allowed to lecture. She is now ranked among the great mathematicians of the twentieth century.
examples: The same experiment on any day gives the same result: energy is conserved.
The same experiment in any room: momentum is conserved.
The same experiment facing any direction: angular momentum is conserved.
explanations.art: A scientist doing the same swinging-weight experiment on a Monday calendar page and on a Tuesday calendar page, with the same result written below each.

explanations.concept: Nature is not the same in a mirror: Chien-Shiung Wu
explanations.definition: In 1957, an experiment led by Chien-Shiung Wu showed that one force inside atoms, the weak force, behaves differently in a mirror world. Nature can tell left from right.
explanations.description: Until 1956, most physicists believed that every law of nature looks the same in a mirror. Two theorists, Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang, suggested that the weak force, which makes some atoms fall apart, might break this rule. They needed someone to test it. Wu, a Chinese-American experimental physicist, cooled radioactive cobalt almost to absolute zero inside a magnet, so the tiny atoms lined up like small spinning tops. Then she and her team counted the electrons flung out by the atoms. More electrons came out in one direction than in the other. In a mirror world, the pattern would be reversed. So a mirror world would not follow our laws. Lee and Yang won the Nobel Prize in 1957. Wu was not included, and many people think she should have been. Her result means we could, in principle, tell someone far away which hand is the left one, with no pictures.
examples: Cobalt atoms line up in a magnet and throw out more electrons one way than the other.
A mirror world would reverse this effect, so it would not be exactly like ours.
Gravity, electricity and magnetism, in contrast, are the same in a mirror.
explanations.art: A cooled block of cobalt inside a magnet coil with a small counter above it and below it, one counting more than the other.

agreed.text: A symmetry of a shape is a move that leaves it looking the same. A regular shape with n equal sides fits back into its outline in 2 times n ways.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can check with a cut-out: turn and flip it in every way and count.

agreed.text: There are exactly seven kinds of border pattern and exactly seventeen kinds of floor pattern.
agreed.evidence: These were proved by mathematics. Fedorov proved the seventeen in 1891 and Pólya found the same result in 1924.

agreed.text: Living bodies use one hand of many molecules. Proteins are made of left-handed amino acids, and the DNA double helix winds to the right.
agreed.evidence: Chemists have measured the handedness of these molecules in laboratories all over the world.

agreed.text: In 1957, an experiment led by Chien-Shiung Wu showed that the weak force is not the same in a mirror.
agreed.evidence: Other laboratories repeated the experiment and got the same result.

agreed.text: Each smooth symmetry in the laws of nature goes with something that is conserved. For example, laws that do not change with time go with conservation of energy.
agreed.evidence: Emmy Noether proved this in 1918. The conservation laws she explained have been tested many times.

agreed.text: Most bodies of animals that move forward are nearly even on the outside but not on the inside. Most people have their heart on the left.
agreed.evidence: Doctors see the position of organs in X-rays and scans. A small number of people have mirrored organs.

challenging.claim: Nature always prefers the most symmetrical shape.
challenging.who: A common idea, and the view of many older thinkers who thought the heavens must be perfect.
challenging.for: Snowflakes, flowers and crystals are very even.
challenging.against: Nature breaks symmetry all the time. A pencil falls, a heart sits on the left, a flatfish has both eyes on one side, and life uses one hand of its molecules.

challenging.claim: A mirror swaps left and right.
challenging.who: Most people. Philosophers and physicists have argued about how to say this properly.
challenging.for: When you raise your right hand, your reflection seems to raise its left hand.
challenging.against: A mirror really swaps front and back, because your nose points towards the mirror and the nose in the mirror points back at you. The left-right swap comes from how you imagine turning round to stand where your reflection stands.

challenging.claim: Quasicrystals are impossible, so Shechtman must have made a mistake.
challenging.who: Many crystal scientists in the 1980s, and the famous chemist Linus Pauling.
challenging.for: Textbooks said that a repeating pattern can only have 2, 3, 4 or 6-fold symmetry, and this is correct for repeating patterns.
challenging.against: Quasicrystals do not repeat, so the rule does not apply to them. Other laboratories found more of them, and natural ones were found in a meteorite. Shechtman won the Nobel Prize in 2011.

challenging.claim: The Alhambra palace in Spain has all 17 kinds of floor pattern.
challenging.for: The Alhambra has many tiling patterns in tile, plaster and carved wood, and some mathematicians have spotted many of the 17 there.
challenging.against: Mathematicians who checked carefully say some of the 17 are missing or hard to find, and the claim is more of a story than a count.

challenging.claim: The left-handed amino acids of life were chosen by the weak force.
challenging.for: The weak force treats left and right differently, so it could give molecules a tiny push towards one hand.
challenging.against: The push is extremely small, and no one has shown that it is big enough to matter. Chance, or a start from space, could explain it equally well.

big_questions.q: When a ruler buckles to the left, was that an accident, or was it decided by something?
big_questions.hint: Think about the tiny bend in the ruler, a tiny difference in your fingers, and whether those are 'causes'.

big_questions.q: Your left hand and right hand are the same in every measurement. In what way are they different?
big_questions.hint: Try to fit your hand outline on top of its twin. What must you do?

big_questions.q: Why might life have chosen only left-handed amino acids?
big_questions.hint: Think about gloves. Would a left-handed glove factory and a right-handed glove factory work well together in one room?

big_questions.q: If someone on another planet describes 'left' in a message, how could they tell us which hand they mean?
big_questions.hint: Photographs and drawings do not help, because we cannot tell which way they are flipped. Chien-Shiung Wu's result gives one way.

big_questions.q: Left-handed people have lived in every age. The world is built mostly for right-handed people. Is that fair, and what could be changed?
big_questions.hint: Think of scissors, desks, can openers and guitars. Who decides what is normal?

big_questions.q: If everything in the universe were perfectly even, would anything have a place or a direction?
big_questions.hint: A line of identical bulbs along a wall. How would you tell one from another if they were truly identical?

big_questions.q: Why do people everywhere make borders and patterns that repeat?
big_questions.hint: Is it easier to make a repeat? Is it pleasing to the eye? Does a repeat tell a story like a rhythm?

big_questions.q: Is it a mistake that your heart sits on the left, or is it how a good body is built?
big_questions.hint: Think of a body with an exactly even inside. Where would the heart and the gut tubes go?

story.title: The Scissors That Would Not Turn
story.note: A made-up story. Left-handed people, scissors that suit one hand, shells that coil one way and the jar lids that tighten to the right are all real. The shop and the family are imagined.
text: Kavya's grandmother had a tailor's shop in Fort Kochi. It was a narrow shop, with a sewing machine by the door and cloth in rolls up to the ceiling. Everyone in the street called her Ammamma.
Every holiday, Kavya's cousin Ayesha came from Hyderabad to stay. Ayesha was nine, the same age as Kavya, and she was left-handed.

This holiday, Ammamma had given them a job. They could cut out cloth squares for a patchwork quilt. Ammamma kept her big black scissors, the shears, on a nail by the machine. Their handles were as long as Kavya's hand.
Kavya cut three squares in a row, easy as paper. Then it was Ayesha's turn.
Ayesha took the shears in her left hand. She lined up the cloth, and squeezed. The cloth slid between the blades and crumpled. She tried again. The blades chewed a ragged edge.
'It's not cutting,' said Ayesha. 'It never cuts. These scissors hate me.'
'You are holding them wrong,' said Kavya. 'Turn them round.'
Ayesha turned them upside down. The blades still slid. She turned them front to back. The blades still slid.
'Try your right hand,' said Kavya.
Ayesha laughed. 'I can't write with my right hand. I can't do anything with my right hand. I can only waste cloth.'
Ammamma came over, looked at the shears, and looked at Ayesha's hand. 'Ah,' she said. 'You need a left-handed pair.' She went to the back of the shop and returned with an old cardboard box.
'A left-handed pair? They look the same,' said Kavya. 'The same handles, the same blades. Why can't she just turn them over?'
'Because turning them over doesn't make them left-handed,' said Ammamma. 'Look closely at the blades.'

Kavya looked. When you close a pair of scissors, one blade passes over the other. On the shears, the top blade was the one on the right side of the handle. In Ayesha's left hand, the squeeze pushed the blades apart, instead of together. The cloth slipped out.

Kavya fetched a piece of paper and traced round the shears. She cut out the shape. She laid it on the table beside the real scissors. Then she flipped her paper shape over, and the top blade jumped to the other side.
'The flip makes a left-handed pair,' she said slowly. 'But I can't flip a real pair of scissors. I can only turn it.'

'That is the trick of it,' said Ammamma. 'A thing and its mirror twin have the same parts, the same size, and the same weight. But you can never turn one into the other. You have to go and make the twin.'
She opened the box. Inside lay a pair of small shears with orange handles. 'My friend's daughter left these here forty years ago. She was left-handed too.'

Ayesha took them in her left hand. The blades came together with a soft snip. The cloth fell away in a clean line. She cut a whole square, then another, and then she kept cutting until the cloth pile was tall.

That evening Kavya found a shell on the windowsill, a small white snail shell from the beach. She turned it in her fingers. Its coil wound to the right, like the thread on a jar lid. She picked up another shell from the jar. It wound to the right too. She went through all twelve. They all wound the same way.
'Almost every snail shell coils the same way,' said Ammamma. 'But now and then a snail is born who coils the other way. Shell collectors prize such a shell.'
Kavya held the shell next to Ayesha's left hand and her own right. 'Everything has a twin,' she said. 'Even a shell.'

The next day, they sat at the shop door sewing the quilt. Ammamma's shears hung on their nail. The small orange pair lay on the table for Ayesha. 'Tomorrow,' said Kavya, 'we ask the whole street who is left-handed. We will find out how many pairs of scissors this street needs.'
Ayesha grinned. 'Start with Ammamma's tailor friends. I bet they have been cutting with the wrong hand for years.'
story.epiphany: A thing and its mirror twin have the same parts, the same size and the same weight, yet no turning can make one into the other. A left-handed person needs a left-handed tool, not the same tool turned round.
ask: Why could Ayesha not just turn the scissors round to cut with her left hand?
What would you need to see to tell that two things are mirror twins?
What is something at home or at school that is built for right-handed people only?
Think of three things that come in a left-handed and a right-handed form.

roots.context: We have counted the moves that leave a shape unchanged, and we have seen that an even start can end lopsided. Now we ask what the pushed strip, the hands and the heart tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: You pushed a straight strip equally from both ends. It still bent to one side. A tiny hidden curve in the strip chose which side. A small difference can turn an even start into a lopsided end.
deep_truth.habit: We think a lopsided result must have come from a lopsided cause of about the same size, so we hunt for the big thing that tipped it. In the strip test the push was even, and the tipping came from a difference too small to see.
deep_truth.evidence: In the strip test, the push at both ends is equal. Card strips like this usually bend mostly one way when flattened, and a strip curled by a coin's thickness usually bends its curled way almost every time. If the strip is turned over, the bend should turn over with it. Only your own tally counts, so write your results down as they are.

three.who_am_i: You began as a ball of cells that looked almost the same on every side. Now your heart is on the left, and scientists think tiny spinning hairs in the early embryo started that difference.
three.what_is_life: The proteins in every living being are built from left-handed amino acids, and the DNA helix winds to the right. Life uses one hand, and nobody knows why.
three.what_is_this_world: In 1957 Chien-Shiung Wu showed that the weak force, one of the basic forces inside atoms, is not the same in a mirror. The world itself can tell left from right.

roots.thread: A pencil on its tip, a pushed strip, an early embryo and the early universe all begin even. Then one tiny difference grows, and a left and a right, a here and a there, appear. Physicists think the early universe was almost perfectly even, and tiny differences grew into stars and galaxies. That is an idea, and not yet settled. What is settled is that you can watch an even start become lopsided with a strip of card. The many shapes of the world come out of sameness through small breaks in it.

teachings.teaching: The Tao gives birth to One. One gives birth to Two. Two gives birth to Three. Three gives birth to all things.
teachings.link: One even start splits into two sides, and the many things come after. A flat strip becomes a bend to one side, and a ball of cells becomes a body with a left and a right.

teachings.teaching: In the beginning there was only Being, one without a second. Being thought, 'May I become many.'
teachings.link: An even beginning is one. The many different shapes and sides come later. Symmetry breaking is the science of how one even start can become many different things.

teachings.source: Aristotle, On the Heavens 2.13, reporting the thinker Anaximander
teachings.teaching: Anaximander is reported to have said that the Earth stays still because it is equally far from everything, so it has no reason to move one way rather than another.
teachings.link: Anaximander used a symmetry argument. In the strip test, equal pushes did leave a decision to be made, and a tiny difference made it.

science.text: Emmy Noether proved in 1918 that every smooth symmetry of the laws of nature goes with something conserved. For example, laws that stay the same over time go with energy that is never lost.
In 1957 an experiment led by Chien-Shiung Wu showed that the weak force is not the same in a mirror.
Why life uses left-handed amino acids and right-handed sugars is not known.

other_view.view: Nothing chooses in symmetry breaking. The laws stay perfectly even, and each possible result is equally allowed. The strip bends because it has to go somewhere, and a tiny difference decides where. No deeper story is needed about sameness becoming many.

practice.title: Even, then a lean
practice.say: Stand with your feet together near a wall. Close your eyes. Feel your weight on both feet. Breathe in slowly. Now breathe out and notice that you sway a tiny bit. Which way do you start to lean? Let the lean happen, and then come back to the middle. Do this three times. Does it lean the same way each time?
practice.kid: Stand near a wall with your eyes closed. Feel both feet. Breathe slowly. Notice which way you start to lean.

ask: The strip was pushed evenly and still bent to one side. What decided which side?
Your two hands are the same in every measurement, yet no turning makes one fit the other. Are they the same or different?
If the early universe was perfectly even, what would it take for anything to be here at all?
roots.art: A card strip bowed to the left in a pair of hands, beside a pencil fallen to the right, a heart drawn on the left of a small body and a left hand and right hand pair.

games.title: Fit-Back Guess: how many ways does it fit?
games.context: This is a number-guessing game about the symmetry count. Each card shows a shape. You guess how many different ways it fits back into its own outline, and then find out.
