printables.title: 10 number tokens for each player: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16 and Endless

rules: Cut out the 24 cards (a parent can do this in advance) and put them in a pile, shape side up, in the printed order for your first game. Every player gets ten number tokens: cut the printed ones, or just write 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 16 and Endless on ten small paper slips. Two to four players is best.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and shows only the front. If a shape is hard to imagine, draw it quickly on scrap paper.
Every other player chooses one number token and puts it face down. Think about turns first, and then flips.
Everyone turns their tokens over together. Then the reader reads the back of the card aloud.
A player with the exact number scores 2 points. A player whose token is the next one along in the row of tokens scores 1 point.
The reader passes the cards to the next player to be the reader. Play until all 24 cards are used, or for 15 minutes.
The player with the most points wins. A tie is a shared win.
Playing alone: be the reader and the player. Choose your token, turn the card, and score yourself. Try to beat your own score next time.

flow.do: Before the game, a parent cuts out the 24 cards. Each player cuts or writes their ten tokens. Keep the cards in the printed order for the first game, so that the triangle and square come first. Shuffle them next time.
flow.say: These cards show shapes. You will guess how many ways each shape fits back into its outline. Each player gets ten number tokens.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Take your ten number tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fit-Back Guess. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. After each card, the reader reads the back aloud and everyone scores their points.
flow.say: The reader shows a shape. Pick a number token and put it face down. Turn them over together. Who is right?
flow.kid: The reader shows a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What do the shapes with the most ways have in common?
good: They have many equal sides.
They look the same from every side.
They are very regular.

flow.parent: Do not tell the count before the guesses. After six cards, the numbers will already look like they follow a pattern.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first six cards and learn how to score.

flow.do: Play the next six cards. Stop after card 12 and ask the question below.
flow.say: Look at the cards so far. The triangle had 6 ways. The square had 8. What do you notice about the number of sides and the number of ways?
flow.kid: Look at the triangle and the square. Count the sides and the ways.

ask.q: What is the link between the number of equal sides and the number of ways?
good: The ways are double the sides.
A triangle has 3 sides and 6 ways. A square has 4 sides and 8 ways.
Turns and flips are each as many as the sides.

flow.context: In this step, you play ten more cards and look for a pattern in the numbers.

flow.do: Play on from card 13 while time allows. Short of time? Jump to the letter F, the letter S, the fan and the hand. Talk about why their counts are low.
flow.say: The letter F and the hand fit in only one way. The S fits in two. Why do these have so few ways?
flow.kid: Look at the F, the S and the hand. Why do they have so few ways?

ask.q: Why does the fan with twisted blades have turns but no flips?
good: A flip would twist the blades the other way.
A flip makes the mirror twin, which is a different fan.

flow.parent: The fan and the pinwheel are handed. A flip turns them into their mirror twins, which are different shapes. Handed shapes have turns only. Playing alone or with a parent, the reader and the player can be the same person. With 3 or 4 children, the reader changes after every card.
flow.context: In this step, you look at the shapes with the lowest counts.

flow.do: Add up the points and name the winner. Ask your child to make up a new card for the next game.
flow.say: Who won? Make a card for the next game. Draw a shape, and work out its count first.
flow.kid: Add up your points. Make a new card with a shape of your own.

check.q: A regular shape has 7 equal sides. How many ways does it fit back into its outline?
check.why: A regular shape with n sides has n turns and n flips. For 7 sides that is 7 plus 7, which is 14. The answer 7 forgets the flips.

flow.context: In this step, you score the game and check what you learned.

experiments.title: Fit-Back Count: how many ways does each shape fit its outline?
experiments.question: How many different ways can each of six cut-out shapes fit back into its own outline? Is there a pattern in the numbers?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many ways will the square fit back into its outline? Which of the six shapes will have the most ways, and which the fewest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every shape is cut from the same card and labelled the same way, with a letter at each corner on both the front and the back. You find the ways the same way each time, by turning and flipping until no new letter pattern appears. Only the shape changes, so differences in the count come from the shape. You check each count twice.

materials.item: a sheet of thin card, such as from a cereal box, about the size of an A4 page
scissors, used by a grown-up or with a grown-up beside the child
a ruler and a sharp pencil
plain paper for tracing the outlines, 3 sheets
a katori lid or a small steel plate about 7 centimetres across, for tracing a circle
a protractor from a geometry box, or 8 centimetres of thread and a pin
a fine pen for writing the corner letters

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the card and pushes the pin. Keep fingers behind the scissors. Put the pin back in its cushion or stick it in an eraser when done.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. For each shape, also write down one of the letter patterns you found, going round the outline from the star. Draw the outline of the square with the star and the letters.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you cut six shapes from card and count how many ways each one can fit back into its own outline. You look for a pattern in your numbers.

setup.art: A square of card, 6 centimetres on each side, being cut from a cereal box with a ruler and scissors beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Cut six shapes from the card: a square, a rectangle, two kinds of half shapes, a circle and a triangle with equal sides.

setup.art: A card square with the letters A, B, C and D written at its four corners, and a second drawing of its back with the same letters at the same corners.
setup.caption: 2. Write a letter at each corner on the front. Flip it over like a page and write the same letters on the back.

setup.art: The square placed on plain paper and its outline traced with a pencil, with a small star at one corner of the outline.
setup.caption: 3. Trace the shape. Put a star at one corner of the outline.

setup.art: The square in its outline, shown four times turned a quarter more each time, with the letters read from the star written under each drawing.
setup.caption: 4. Fit the shape back. Read the letters clockwise from the star. Write them down.

setup.art: The square flipped over and fitted back in the outline, with new letter patterns written beside the first four.
setup.caption: 5. Flip the shape over and fit it back. Write every new letter pattern.

flow.do: Show your child a card square and its outline. Ask them to guess how many ways it fits back. Write the guesses for all six shapes in the table.
flow.say: Here is a square and its outline. How many different ways can it fit back in? Which of our six shapes will have the most ways? Which will have the fewest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many ways the square fits its outline. Which shape fits most ways? Why?

ask.q: Which shape do you think has the most ways, and why?
good: The circle, because it looks the same however you turn it.
The square, because it has four equal sides.
The one with the most corners.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write them at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Fit-Back Count. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the six shapes from the card. First, a square 6 centimetres on each side. Second, a rectangle 8 centimetres by 4 centimetres. Third, a second square cut along its diagonal into two triangles, and keep one. Fourth, a second rectangle cut along its diagonal, and keep one half. Fifth, a circle traced round the katori lid. Sixth, a triangle with three sides of 8 centimetres each.
flow.say: A grown-up cuts these shapes for us. The triangle has three equal sides. It is the one that needs care.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut six shapes. Look at each one when it is ready.
flow.parent: For the triangle with equal sides, draw an 8 centimetre line. At each end, use the protractor to draw a 60 degree line upwards. They meet at the third corner. With no protractor, tie a thread to a pencil, hold the 8 centimetre end at one end of the line with a pin, and draw an arc. Repeat from the other end. The arcs cross at the third corner. The diagonal cuts of the square and the rectangle give a triangle with two equal sides and a triangle with all sides different.
flow.context: In this step, you make the six shapes from card.

flow.do: On the front of each shape, write the letter A at one corner. Write B, C and D going round. Turn each shape over like a page. Write the same letters at the same corners on the back. Trace each shape on paper. Put a star at one corner of each outline.
flow.say: Every corner gets a letter on both sides. That way we can tell the fits apart. The star on the outline tells us where to start reading.
flow.kid: Write letters at the corners on both sides. Trace each shape. Add a star.
flow.parent: The circle only needs one dot on its edge. For the triangles, use only the letters A, B and C. Write the letters small and clear with a dark pen on the plain grey inside of the cereal box card, so they show at the corners.

check.q: Why do we write the letters on both sides of each shape?
options: So that we can tell the fits apart when the shape is flipped over
So that the shape looks neat
So that the shape is heavier
check.why: When a shape is flipped, we see its back. If the back had no letters, we could not tell which corner is which, and we could not tell one fit from another.

flow.context: In this step, you label the corners and trace the outlines. This lets you tell the different fits apart.

flow.do: Put the square in its outline. Read the letters clockwise from the star and write them down. Turn the square a quarter turn. Write the new letters. Keep going until you have all the fits from turning. Then flip it over and do the same again.
flow.say: Read the corner letters from the star, going clockwise. Turn it a quarter. Read again. How many different patterns do you find?
flow.kid: Read the letters from the star. Turn the square. Read again. Then flip it.
flow.parent: The four turns give ABCD, DABC, CDAB and BCDA, in some order of reading. The flipped square gives four more, which read in the opposite order, such as ADCB. A pattern counts once. The letters on the star corner and the order show which is new.

check.q: You found 4 ways to fit the square by turning. You then flipped it over and found more. How many ways in all?
check.why: Each of the 4 turns can be done with the front up or with the back up. That makes 4 times 2, which is 8. Only 4 would mean forgetting the flips.

flow.context: In this step, you find all the ways the square fits back and write the letter patterns.

flow.do: Do the same for the other five shapes. For each shape, write every different letter pattern. Stop when no new pattern appears after every turn and flip. Fill in the table. For the circle, write endless.
flow.say: Find the fits for each shape. Turn and flip it every way. Stop when nothing new appears. Write the count in the table.
flow.kid: Find the fits for each shape. Turn and flip. Write the counts in the table.

ask.q: Which shape surprised you?
good: The scalene triangle, which fits in only one way.
The circle, which has no end.
The rectangle, which has fewer than the square.

flow.parent: Expect: square 8, rectangle 4, equal-sided triangle 6, triangle with two equal sides 2, triangle with three different sides 1, circle endless. If a count is odd, check for a letter pattern counted twice, or a shape that did not fit properly. The triangle with three different sides has only the start pattern. With 2 to 4 children: one child turns and flips, one reads the letters from the star, and one writes them down. Swap roles for each shape. Each pair or group needs only one set of shapes, but a second child can cut a spare square to check the count on their own.
flow.context: In this step, you find the fits for the other five shapes.

flow.do: Look at the table. Ask your child for a claim, the evidence and the reason. Ask them to look at the square and the triangle with three equal sides.
flow.say: What did you find? What did you see in the numbers? Why do you think the count is the way it is? Look at the equal-sided shapes. What is the link between sides and ways?
flow.kid: What did you find? What numbers show it? Why does it happen?

ask.q: What is the link between the number of equal sides and the number of ways?
good: The number of ways is double the number of sides.
The triangle has 3 sides and 6 ways. The square has 4 sides and 8 ways.
There are as many turns as sides and as many flips as sides.

flow.parent: A strong answer says: the equal-sided shapes have as many fits by turning as they have sides, and the same number again by flipping. So the count is double the number of sides. Shapes with unequal sides have fewer. A shape that is not the same as its mirror twin has no flip that fits.

check.q: A shape with 5 equal sides and 5 equal angles fits back into its outline in how many ways?
check.why: There are 5 turns and 5 flips, which gives 10. If you answered 5, you counted the turns and forgot the flips.

flow.context: In this step, you look for the pattern in your table and say what you found.

experiments.title: The Pushed Strip: which way does it bend?
experiments.question: When you push a straight card strip evenly from both ends, which way does it bend? Is it the same each time? What decides?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When you push the ends of a straight strip together, will the middle bend towards you, away from you, or sometimes each way? Will a curled strip behave differently? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use strips of the same card, the same length and the same width. Push slowly, with the same hands, in the same way each time. Do ten tries for each strip. Change only the strip. Flatten the strip between tries so the last bend does not set the next.

materials.item: thin card, such as from a cereal box, cut into 3 strips 20 centimetres long and 2 centimetres wide
scissors and a ruler
a pencil with a smooth round side, for curling the strips
a pen to mark a dot on each strip
a one-rupee coin, for measuring how much the strips are curled
a flat table to rest the strips on between tries

experiments.safety: Keep the strip away from your face and eyes when you push it. Push slowly. Fold over any sharp corner of card.
experiments.record: Make a tally mark in the table for every try. Draw one strip bent towards you and one bent away, seen from above, with the dot on the side facing you.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you push card strips from both ends and see which way they bend. You find what decides the direction when the push is the same from both ends.

setup.art: Three card strips on a table beside a pair of scissors and a ruler, each with a dot drawn in the middle of one face.
setup.caption: 1. Cut three strips 20 centimetres long and 2 centimetres wide. Draw a dot in the middle of one face of each.

setup.art: A card strip pulled gently over the side of a pencil, curling it so that the dotted side is on the inside of the curve.
setup.caption: 2. Curl strip B gently over a pencil, with the dot on the inside. Curl strip C with the dot on the outside.

setup.art: A card strip held upright by two hands at its ends, with the dot facing the child, and the strip bowing towards the child.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the strip upright with the dot facing you. Push the ends slowly together.

setup.art: A tally table with three rows labelled A, B and C and two columns, towards me and away from me, with tally marks in each box.
setup.caption: 4. Make a tally mark for each try.

flow.do: Show the card, a strip and the pencil. Ask your child to guess and give a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will push a straight strip from both ends, evenly. Which way will the middle bend, towards you or away from you? Will it be the same every time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Push a straight strip from both ends. Which way will it bend? Why?

ask.q: Which way will a straight strip bend, and why?
good: It will bend either way, because both sides are the same.
It will go towards me, because I am pushing.
It will go the same way each time.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say it will go in any direction at random. Others say it must go straight. All guesses with a reason are good.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pushed Strip test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Cut the three strips (a grown-up helps younger children with the scissors). Mark a dot in the middle of one face of each strip. Write A, B and C at one end. Flatten strip A by rubbing it along the edge of the table in both directions until it lies flat. Curl strip B over the pencil with the dot on the inside. Curl strip C the other way.
flow.say: Strip A is flat. Strip B is curled towards the dot. Strip C is curled away from the dot. Lay each on the table. A curl the thickness of a coin at the ends is enough.
flow.kid: Cut three strips and mark a dot. Flatten A. Curl B and C gently.
flow.parent: A gentle curl is enough. Lay the strip on the table. Its ends should lift about the thickness of a one-rupee coin. If the strip creases, throw it away and cut a new one. A crease is a sharp fold and spoils the test.
flow.context: In this step, you make the three strips. One is flattened and two are curled in opposite ways.

flow.do: Take strip A. Hold it upright with the dot facing you and an end in each hand. Push the ends slowly together until the middle bends. Note which way the middle goes. Make a tally mark. Lay the strip flat and rub it flat again. Do ten tries.
flow.say: Hold the strip with the dot facing you. Push the ends slowly together. Which way does the middle go? Mark it down. Flatten the strip each time.
flow.kid: Hold strip A with the dot facing you. Push the ends together. Where does the middle go?

ask.q: Did strip A bend the same way each time?
good: Mostly the same way.
Sometimes one way and sometimes the other.
Always towards me.

flow.parent: A flattened card strip is rarely perfectly flat. Many children find strip A goes mostly one way, which tells us it has a hidden tiny curve. If it goes both ways about equally, that is a fine result too. Write what you see. Pinch the ends flat between thumb and finger, keep the strip upright, and push until the middle has moved about 3 centimetres. Stop before it creases. If the strip folds sideways on its edge, it is too wide: trim it a little.
flow.context: In this step, you push the flattened strip ten times and tally which way it bends.

flow.do: Test strip B ten times in the same way, with the dot facing you. Then test strip C ten times. Make a tally mark each time.
flow.say: Now the curled strips. B is curled with the dot inside. C is curled with the dot outside. Hold each with the dot facing you. Do ten tries each. Which way do they go?
flow.kid: Test strip B ten times. Test strip C ten times. Tally each try.

ask.q: What happened with the curled strips?
good: They went the same way every time.
B went one way and C went the other way.

flow.parent: Expect strip B (dot on the inside, facing you) to bow away from you almost every time, and strip C to bow towards you almost every time. The curl is the tiny difference that decides. If a curled strip does not go the same way at least 8 times out of 10, curl it a little more. Numbers will vary a little from family to family. With 2 to 4 children: each child makes their own set of A, B and C and does the tries. A second child tallies. Then put all the tallies together in one table.

check.q: Strip B is curled towards the dot and bends the same way ten times out of ten. What is the best explanation?
options: The curl in the strip decides which way it bends
Your left hand is stronger than your right
The dot is heavy
check.why: The strip has a hidden curve, and the push makes it bend more along that curve. If your left hand were deciding, strip C would bend the same way as strip B. The dot is just a pen mark and has almost no weight.

flow.context: In this step, you test the two curled strips ten times each.

flow.do: Take strip A again. Turn it over so the dot faces away from you. Push the ends together six times. Tally the bends.
flow.say: Now turn strip A over. The dot faces away from you. Does it bend towards you or away from you this time?
flow.kid: Turn strip A over. Push it six times. Does it bend the same way?

ask.q: When you turned strip A over, did it bend the same way as before?
good: No, it flipped to the other way.
Yes, it still goes towards me.

flow.parent: If strip A bends the opposite way after turning over, its own hidden curve decided. If it still bends the same way, your hands or the way you stand may be deciding. Both are real results.
flow.context: In this step, you turn strip A over to find out whether the strip or your hands decide.

flow.do: Look at the table. Ask your child for a claim, the evidence and the reason. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: What did you find? What numbers show it? Why do you think a perfectly even push gave a lopsided bend? What decided which way?
flow.kid: What did you find? What numbers show it? What decided the bend?

ask.q: The push was the same at both ends. Why did the strip bend to one side?
good: The strip has a tiny curve that decides.
A tiny difference in the strip made it go one way.
It had to go one way, and the tiny curve picked it.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses the numbers: strip A mostly went one way, B and C went opposite ways every time, and turning A over changed its direction. The reasoning is that an even push has no side to favour, so a tiny difference in the strip does. Scientists call this symmetry breaking. Some other words children use are fine.

check.q: You push a flat strip evenly from both ends and it bows towards the dot 8 times out of 10. What is the most likely reason?
options: The strip has a tiny hidden curve that favours that side
Your push was much stronger at one end
Strips always bend towards the dot
check.why: An even push leaves both sides equally possible, so something tiny must decide. A hidden curve fits best. A much stronger push at one end would not make the same bend each time. Strips do not know where the dot is.

flow.context: In this step, you say what you found and why an even push gave a lopsided result.

activities.title: Stamp a Border: five moves, five borders

materials.item: a card stencil of the capital letter F, about 4 centimetres tall, cut out by a grown-up from a cereal box or old file cover
5 strips of plain paper, each about 30 centimetres long and 10 centimetres wide (cut an A4 sheet lengthwise in two)
a pencil and a ruler
coloured pencils
a saree, a dupatta, a bedsheet with a printed border, or a picture of a temple wall, for the hunt

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts out the F stencil.

schedule.what: Make five borders with the F stencil, one for each move. Then hunt for the same moves on a real border.

activities.record: Stick your five borders in a column in your notebook. Write the name of the move beside each one: slide, flip across, flip along, half turn or glide.
activities.context: In this activity, you build five border patterns from the letter F using one move each time. You then look for the same moves on a saree or a temple wall.

setup.art: A card stencil of the letter F lying on a paper strip, and a row of F shapes traced along the strip, each one slid to the right.
setup.caption: 1. Trace the F, slide the stencil along, and trace it again, five times. This is a slide border.

setup.art: Five paper strips stacked one above the other, each with a row of F shapes: sliding, flipped left and right, flipped up and down, turned half way round and glided.
setup.caption: 2. Make four more borders. Each uses a different move: flip across, flip along, half turn, or glide.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts out an F stencil from card. Show your child the five moves with the stencil on the table. Ask them to say what each move does.
flow.say: This F can do five things. It can slide. It can flip over a line across the border. It can flip over a line along the border. It can turn halfway. It can glide, which is a flip and a slide together. What will a row of slid Fs look like?
flow.kid: The F can slide, flip, turn and glide. What will a row of slid Fs look like?

ask.q: What will a border made by sliding the F look like?
good: The same F again and again, all facing the same way.
Like a row of the same picture.
Like a train.

flow.parent: Cut the F from stiff card so it can be traced many times. The F has no symmetry of its own. That makes every move easy to see.
flow.context: This is the first step of Stamp a Border. You get the F stencil and meet the five moves.

flow.do: Border one: trace the F at the left of a strip. Slide the stencil 6 centimetres to the right. Trace it again. Do this five times. Border two: trace the F. Flip the stencil like a page, so it faces the other way, and trace it beside the first. Keep flipping and tracing along the strip.
flow.say: Border one is a slide. Every F faces the same way. Border two flips over a line across the strip, like a page. The Fs take turns facing left and right.
flow.kid: Slide the F and trace it five times. Then trace an F, flip it, and trace again.

check.q: A border has the same F again and again, all facing the same way, each one further along. Which move made it?
options: A slide
A flip
A half turn
check.why: When every copy is the same way up and facing the same way, it was slid along. A flip would turn some copies the other way round, and a half turn would turn some upside down.

flow.context: In this step, you make the first two borders: a slide border and a flip across.

flow.do: First draw a pencil line along the middle of the strips for borders three and five. Border three: trace the F above the line. Flip the stencil upside down over the line, and trace it directly below the first F. Slide the stencil 6 centimetres along and trace the pair again. Border four: trace the F. Turn the stencil halfway round and trace it beside the first. Repeat. Border five: trace the F above the line. Flip the stencil upside down and trace it below the line, but shifted 3 centimetres along. Keep going, alternating above and below.
flow.say: Border three flips each F over the middle line, so every F has an upside-down twin below it. Border four turns the F halfway round, so it is upside down but not flipped. Border five is the glide. It flips over the line and slides along at the same time, so the Fs zigzag.
flow.kid: Make three more borders. One flips the F upside down. One turns it halfway. One does both a flip and a slide.
flow.parent: Children often mix up the flip and the half turn. A flip makes a mirror image. A half turn does not. Look at the F: a half-turned F is still a proper F, but upside down. A flipped F reads backwards. If two borders look the same, one may have been done wrong. Try again with the stencil.
flow.context: In this step, you make the other three borders: a flip along, a half turn and a glide.

flow.do: Stick the five borders in a column. Write the move beside each one. Ask your child which two borders look most alike and which move differs.
flow.say: Put your borders in a column. Write the name of the move next to each. Which two look most alike? Which move is different?
flow.kid: Put your five borders in a column. Name the move for each.

ask.q: Which borders look most alike, and what is different?
good: The half turn and the glide, but the half turn is not flipped.
The two flip borders, but one flips across and the other flips along.

flow.parent: There are seven kinds of border altogether. These five moves make five of them. The other two are made by mixing moves, such as a flip across and a half turn together. With 2 to 4 children: each child makes one or two borders. Then each hides the move name and the others guess it from the strip.
flow.context: In this step, you collect your five borders and name the move for each.

flow.do: Look at a saree border, a bedsheet, a temple picture or a floor tile edge. For each, find the repeating unit. Decide which move takes one unit to the next.
flow.say: Find a real border. What is the shape that repeats? Does it slide, flip, turn or glide? Try covering all but two units with your hand to see.
flow.kid: Find a real border. What repeats? Is it a slide, a flip, a turn or a glide?

ask.q: Which move does your real border use?
good: A slide. The same shape is repeated along.
A flip. Mangoes face one way and then the other.
A glide. Leaves point up and down alternately.

flow.parent: Most simple borders on cloth are slides. Borders with pairs of animals or birds facing each other use a flip across. Alternating up and down shapes use a glide. Do not worry if the real border looks messy. Pick the move that matches best.
flow.context: In this step, you find the same moves on a real border.

activities.title: Two Mirrors: how many copies do you see?

materials.item: 2 small flat mirrors of the same size, about 8 centimetres wide, such as compact mirrors or mirror tiles
tape, to hinge the mirrors together and to cover the edges
a small coloured object, such as an eraser or a bindi, to stand between the mirrors
a sheet of plain paper
a protractor, or the equal-sided triangle card from the Fit-Back Count, whose corner is 60 degrees
a lump of atta dough or clay (or two books), to prop the mirrors upright

activities.safety: Glass mirrors can cut. A grown-up covers all the edges with tape, or use plastic mirrors. Do not drop them. Do not put the mirrors where they could reflect strong sunlight into anyone's eyes. Do not let the sun through a window shine on the mirrors while you work.

schedule.what: Hinge two mirrors, set them at different angles, count the objects you see, and find the rule.

activities.record: A table with the angle, your guess, the number of objects you counted, and 360 divided by the angle.
activities.context: In this activity, you hinge two mirrors and set them at an angle. You count how many copies of an object you see and find the rule that links the count to the angle.

setup.art: Two small mirrors laid face up side by side and joined along one edge by a strip of tape, like a book hinge.
setup.caption: 1. Tape two mirrors together along one edge to make a hinge.

setup.art: Two hinged mirrors standing open at a right angle on a sheet of paper with a small coloured eraser between them, and a child looking in from above.
setup.caption: 2. Stand them open at 90 degrees with the object in between. Count the objects you see.

setup.art: A sheet with lines drawn from one point at 120, 90, 60 and 45 degrees to each other, with the hinge standing on one angle.
setup.caption: 3. Open the mirrors to different angles using the lines on the sheet.

flow.do: Draw four angles on the sheet, with the same corner point. Use 120, 90, 60 and 45 degrees. Ask your child to guess how many objects they will see at each angle.
flow.say: We will put one small object between two mirrors. How many objects will you see in all, counting the real one? Guess for 90 degrees, then 60, then 45. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many objects you will see between two mirrors. Why?

ask.q: How many objects will you see at 90 degrees, and why?
good: Two, one real and one in the mirror.
Four, because the mirrors also reflect each other.
More as the angle gets smaller.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children guess 2 for every angle. The answers are 3, 4, 6 and 8 for 120, 90, 60 and 45 degrees. Draw 90 degrees from the corner of the paper, 45 by folding that corner in half, 60 from the corner of the equal-sided card triangle, and 120 with a protractor (or by drawing two 60 degree angles side by side).
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two Mirrors test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Tape the two mirrors together along one edge, with the shiny sides facing each other. Cover the other edges with tape.
flow.say: Lay the mirrors face up side by side. Tape them along one edge. Now the mirrors can open and close like a book.
flow.kid: Tape the two mirrors together. Cover the edges with tape.
flow.parent: Press the tape firmly on both mirrors so the hinge is stiff but can still move. The mirrors must meet exactly at the hinge. A gap makes the pattern harder to see.
flow.context: In this step, you make the mirror hinge.

flow.do: Stand the mirrors on the sheet, with the hinge on the corner point and the mirrors along the 90 degree lines. Put the object between them, close to the hinge. Look in from above. Count the objects in all, including the real one.
flow.say: Open the mirrors to a right angle. Put the object near the hinge. Look in from above. How many objects can you count, including the real one?
flow.kid: Open the mirrors to 90 degrees. Count all the objects you see. Include the real one.

check.q: At 90 degrees, how many objects do you see in all, including the real one?
check.why: Each mirror shows one copy, and the two mirrors also reflect each other's copy. That makes the real one plus three copies, which is 4 in all.

flow.parent: Place the object close to the hinge. Count only objects that look complete. At 90 degrees you should see 4: the real one and 3 copies. Prop the mirrors upright with a little dough at the foot. With 2 to 4 children: one child holds the mirrors and moves the object, and each other child counts on their own, then you compare. If counts differ, the mirrors are not sitting exactly on the lines. Cheap glass mirrors show a faint second image because of the glass. Count the bright ones.
flow.context: In this step, you set the mirrors at 90 degrees and count the objects.

flow.do: Open the mirrors to 120, 60 and 45 degrees in turn. Each time, count all the objects and write the number. Work out 360 divided by the angle.
flow.say: Now 120 degrees, then 60, then 45. Count all the objects each time. Write the number. Then work out 360 divided by the angle. Is there a link?
flow.kid: Try 120, 60 and 45 degrees. Count the objects each time. Work out 360 divided by the angle.

ask.q: What link do you see between the angle and the number of objects?
good: A smaller angle gives more objects.
The number of objects is 360 divided by the angle.
At 90 degrees it is 4 and at 45 degrees it is 8.

flow.parent: Expect 3, 4, 6 and 8 objects. They match 360 divided by 120, 90, 60 and 45. At small angles the copies get hard to see. Count the ones you can see clearly.
flow.context: In this step, you try three more angles and look for the rule.

flow.do: Peel off the tape. Stand each mirror upright in dough, 10 centimetres apart, shiny sides facing, with the object between. Look along the gap from slightly above. Count the objects.
flow.say: Now stand the mirrors face to face, with the object in the middle. How many objects can you see?
flow.kid: Put the mirrors face to face. Look along the gap. How many objects do you see?

ask.q: What happens to the number of objects when the mirrors face each other?
good: There are too many to count.
It goes on and on.
It is endless.

flow.parent: Parallel mirrors give a long row of copies, each one a little fainter and smaller, that seem to go on for ever. This is like the angle being zero, which gives an endless count.
flow.context: In this step, you place the mirrors face to face and see an endless row.

flow.do: Ask your child to link the result to the order of rotational symmetry from Class 3.
flow.say: The objects you saw formed a pattern that matches itself when turned. What was its order of rotational symmetry at 60 degrees?
flow.kid: At 60 degrees, how often does the pattern match in a full turn?

check.q: Two mirrors are set at 72 degrees. What number does 360 divided by the angle give, and what does it tell you?
options: 5, the number of objects seen in all
72, the number of mirrors
288, the number of turns
check.why: 360 divided by 72 is 5. The mirrors make 5 objects in all, arranged round the hinge. That is the order of rotational symmetry of the pattern.

flow.context: In this step, you link the mirror pattern to the order of rotational symmetry.

activities.title: Left, Right or Both? A handedness hunt

materials.item: 2 sheets of plain thin paper that you can see through, such as tracing paper or thin notebook paper, and a thick dark pen
scissors and a pencil
as many things with a screw thread as you can find, at least 6: jar lids, bottle caps, pen caps or tube caps, and a nut and bolt if you have them
a piece of rope, string or thick thread with a visible twist
a pair of gloves, chappals or shoes
a snail shell or a shankha, if you have one

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors for younger children. Test only lids and caps that are safe to open. Look at gas cylinder valves, but do not touch or turn them.

schedule.what: Test letters, hands, screw threads and rope twists to find which things are handed.

activities.record: A table with two columns: 'Same as its mirror image' and 'Handed'. Write each thing you test in the right column.
activities.context: In this activity, you test letters, hands, lids and ropes to find which are handed and which are not. You find out which way familiar things twist.

setup.art: The capital letters F, A, S and H written large on thin paper, and one sheet held up to a window and seen from behind.
setup.caption: 1. Write letters big. Hold the paper to a window and look from the back.

setup.art: A left hand traced on paper and cut out, laid on the traced outline of a right hand.
setup.caption: 2. Trace your left hand and cut it out. Try it on the outline of your right hand.

setup.art: A hand turning a jar lid clockwise, with a curved arrow, and a rope with a diagonal twist shown close up.
setup.caption: 3. Turn each lid to tighten it. Look at the twist in the rope.

flow.do: Write the capital letters F, A, S, H, R and T big and dark on thin paper. Hold the paper up to a window. Look at each letter from the back. Sort the letters into 'looks the same from the back' and 'looks reversed'.
flow.say: Write each letter big and dark. Hold the page to the window and look from the back. Which letters look the same? Which look reversed?
flow.kid: Write six big letters. Look at them from the back. Which look the same?

ask.q: Which letters look the same from the back, and which look reversed?
good: A, H and T look the same.
F, S and R look reversed.

flow.parent: A, H and T look the same, because each has a line of symmetry. F, S and R look reversed. A letter that looks different from the back is handed in a flat drawing.

check.q: A flat shape looks reversed when you see it from the back. What does that tell you?
options: It has no line of symmetry, so it is handed
It is a bad shape
It is too thin
check.why: If a shape has a line of symmetry, its back view looks just the same. If its back view looks reversed, no fold line matches its halves, and the shape is handed.

flow.context: In this step, you test letters from the back to find which ones are handed.

flow.do: Trace both of your hands on paper, left and right, with fingers spread. Cut out the left hand. Try to fit the cut-out onto the outline of your right hand, with the same side up. Then flip the cut-out over and try again.
flow.say: Trace your left hand and cut it out. Lay it on the outline of your right hand. Does it fit? Now flip it over. What happens?
flow.kid: Cut out your left hand. Try it on your right-hand outline. Then flip it.

ask.q: What happens when you flip the cut-out of your left hand?
good: It fits the right-hand outline.
It becomes a right hand.

flow.parent: The cut-out of a left hand fits the right-hand outline only after it is flipped over. A real hand cannot be flipped, so a real left hand never fits a right-hand glove.
flow.context: In this step, you test your own hands as cut-outs.

flow.do: For each lid, bottle cap and screw, find which way you turn it to tighten it. Look from above at the lid. Write clockwise or anticlockwise. Look at the twist of the rope. Does it slope like the middle of an S or like the middle of a Z?
flow.say: Turn each lid to tighten it. Which way is it, clockwise or anticlockwise? Write it down. Then look at the twist in the rope. Does it slope like an S or a Z?
flow.kid: Turn each lid to tighten it. Is it clockwise or anticlockwise? Look at the rope twist.

ask.q: Which way did most of the lids tighten?
good: Clockwise.
All the same way.

flow.parent: Nearly every screw thread tightens clockwise when seen from above. This is a rule people agreed on, so tools fit everywhere. A few things, such as some gas cylinder valves, use the other hand on purpose, to avoid mistakes. A rope is made of strands twisted one way and then twisted together the other way, so the twist you see depends on the rope. Tally the clockwise and anticlockwise lids in a table. Almost all should be clockwise. With 2 to 4 children: each child tests different lids from the kitchen, and you pool the tally. Do not force a stuck lid.
flow.context: In this step, you test screw threads and rope twists to find out which way they wind.

flow.do: Look at a snail shell or a picture of one. Hold it with the tip pointing up and the opening facing you. Do the coils wind to the right or to the left? Look at a hair whorl on the back of the head of a family member. Is it clockwise or anticlockwise? Ask five people and write the numbers.
flow.say: Look at the shell with the tip up and the opening facing you. Which way do the coils go? Now look at the swirl of hair at the back of someone's head. Which way does it spin?
flow.kid: Look at a shell and hair swirls. Which way do they wind?

ask.q: What did you notice about the hair swirls of five people?
good: Most went the same way.
They were not all the same.
Mine went clockwise.

flow.parent: Most snail shells coil one way, so a shell that coils the other way is a rare find. For hair swirls, more people are clockwise than anticlockwise, but both are common. Both directions are normal in people. Report what you find. If you have no shell, search for a picture.
flow.context: In this step, you look at a shell and at hair swirls.

activities.title: A Tile That Tiles: cut a bump and slide it across

materials.item: a square of card, 6 centimetres on each side
scissors and clear tape
a pencil
a big sheet of plain paper
coloured pencils

activities.safety: A grown-up helps younger children with the scissors.

schedule.what: Cut a bump from the square, tape it to the opposite side, and use the new tile to cover a whole sheet with no gaps.

activities.record: Stick your finished tiling in your notebook. Draw the tile on its own. Write: which move did I use to make the tile, and which move did I use to cover the page?
activities.context: In this activity, you change a square tile into a curvy shape that still covers a flat sheet with no gaps. You find which move keeps the tiling working.

setup.art: A card square with a small curved bump cut from the top side and taped to the bottom side, so the square has a dent on top and a bump on the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a curvy piece from the top side. Slide it straight down and tape it to the bottom side.

setup.art: The same tile with a second curved bump cut from the left side and taped to the right side.
setup.caption: 2. Cut another piece from the left side. Slide it across and tape it to the right side.

setup.art: A big sheet covered with traced copies of the curvy tile, fitting together with no gaps, and some drawn with eyes and a tail to look like creatures.
setup.caption: 3. Trace the tile again and again, sliding it to fit. Colour the shapes.

flow.do: Show your child the square. Ask whether a curvy shape cut from the square could still cover a page with no gaps.
flow.say: Squares cover a page with no gaps. If I change the shape of the square with a curvy cut, could it still cover a page with no gaps? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Squares cover a page with no gaps. Will a curvy tile?

ask.q: Do you think a curvy tile can still cover a page with no gaps?
good: Yes, if what I cut out goes back in somewhere.
No, curvy shapes leave gaps.
Maybe, if the bumps and dents match.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good. The trick is that the piece you cut away is added back on the opposite side.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Tile That Tiles. You guess before you try.

flow.do: Cut a curvy piece from the middle of the top side of the square. Do not cut it off the tile completely at the corners. Slide the piece straight down to the bottom side. Tape it there, with the cut edge outwards. Do the same with a piece from the left side to the right side.
flow.say: Cut a curvy piece from the top. Slide it straight down without turning it. Tape it to the bottom. Now do the same from the left to the right.
flow.kid: Cut a bump from the top. Slide it to the bottom. Tape it. Do it from the left to the right.
flow.parent: The piece must slide without turning or flipping. Keep its curved edge matching the edge it was cut from. Keep the bump and dent shapes simple. Too many wiggles make the tracing hard.
flow.context: In this step, you change the square into a curvy tile by sliding two pieces across.

flow.do: Trace the tile in one corner of the big sheet. Slide the tile to fit against the first one. Trace it again. Keep going until the sheet is covered, with no gaps and no overlaps.
flow.say: Trace the tile. Slide it so its bump fits into the next dent. Trace it again. Do not turn it. Keep going over the whole page.
flow.kid: Trace the tile. Slide it so the bump fits a dent. Trace again.

check.q: Why does the curvy tile leave no gaps when you slide it?
options: Every bump you cut off was added back as a matching bump on the opposite side
Curvy shapes always tile
The paper stretches
check.why: The piece cut from one side was moved to the opposite side without changing its shape. So each dent matches a bump of the neighbouring tile, and nothing is missing. Not every curvy shape would work this way.

flow.context: In this step, you cover the sheet with copies of the tile.

flow.do: Colour the tiles so they look like creatures. Add eyes, tails or wings.
flow.say: Now make your tile a creature. What does the bump look like? A tail? A nose? Draw an eye.
flow.kid: Colour your tiles. Make them into creatures.

ask.q: What creature did your tile become?
good: A bird.
A fish.
A dragon.

flow.parent: The artist M. C. Escher became famous for making tilings of birds, fish and lizards from tiles like this. He worked on many of them with simple shapes cut and slid in the same way.
flow.context: In this step, you turn the tiles into creatures.

flow.do: Count how many tiles covered your sheet. Compare with the number of plain 6 centimetre squares that would cover it (about 17 for a whole A4 sheet). Ask your child to say which move covered the page, and which move made the tile.
flow.say: How many tiles covered the sheet? About how many plain squares would it take? Which move did you use to make the tile from the square? Which move covered the page? What would a flip do instead?
flow.kid: Which move made the tile? Which move covered the page?

ask.q: Which move covered the page, and which move made the tile?
good: Sliding covered the page and sliding the pieces made the tile.
Sliding for both.

flow.parent: Both moves are slides. A slide keeps every copy the same way up, so bumps and dents always meet. The count of tiles should be about the same as the count of squares, because the piece was moved, not thrown away. Edge tiles that run off the sheet make the count only approximate. With 2 to 4 children: each child cuts and tapes their own tile, then all tile one big sheet together, or swap tiles and try each other's.
flow.context: In this step, you name the moves that made and covered the tiling.

projects.title: The Symmetry Notebook: four days of finding

materials.item: a notebook and a pencil
a ruler, for dotted mirror lines
coloured pencils
a phone camera, if you have one, for photographing borders
tracing paper or thin paper for testing flips

schedule.what: Find three things with a line of symmetry and one thing with none. Draw them with dotted lines.
Find one real border pattern at home or nearby and name the move that repeats it.
Find three handed things, and one thing that has a mirror twin you could buy.
Find one thing that is lopsided on purpose, and write how the lopsided part helps.

projects.record: Four notebook pages, one for each day, with drawings and a sentence on each.
projects.context: In this project, you spend four short days looking for different kinds of symmetry around you. Each day has a question, and you keep your finds in a notebook.

setup.art: A notebook page headed Day 1 with three drawings, a butterfly, a leaf and a katori, each with a dotted mirror line.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: draw three things with a mirror line, and mark the line.

setup.art: A saree border photographed with a pencil arrow showing how its unit repeats.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: find a border, and draw an arrow for the move that repeats it.

setup.art: A pair of chappals, a pair of gloves and a jar lid drawn on a page headed Day 3, with the words left and right.

flow.say: Find three things with a line of symmetry. Draw them and add the dotted line. Find one thing with none. How do you test it?
flow.kid: Find three things with a mirror line. Draw each one. Add the line.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Symmetry Notebook. You find mirror lines.
flow.parent: Each child keeps their own notebook. With 2 to 4 children, compare finds at the end of each day. Never touch live animals or pick up sharp tools while hunting. Look and draw only.

flow.do: On day 2, find a real border pattern, such as a saree border, a tile edge or a carving in a picture. Draw one unit and an arrow showing how it repeats. Write the name of the move.
flow.say: Find a border today. What is the unit that repeats? Does it slide, flip, turn or glide? Draw an arrow.
flow.kid: Find a border. What repeats? Draw an arrow. Name the move.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Symmetry Notebook. You find a border pattern.

flow.do: On day 3, find three handed things, such as a left and right chappal, gloves or a jar lid. Write whether each one tightens or fits left or right. Find one pair that you can buy as left and right.
flow.say: Find three handed things today. How do you know they are handed? Can you buy the twin of each?
flow.kid: Find three things that come in a left and a right. Draw them.
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Symmetry Notebook. You find handed things.

flow.say: Find something lopsided that has a good reason to be lopsided. What does the lopsided part do? Read your pages aloud.
flow.kid: Find something lopsided on purpose. Why is it lopsided? Read your pages aloud.

check.q: A flounder has both eyes on the same side of the head. What does this give her?
options: A flat body that rests on the sea floor and still sees upwards
More food
A faster swim
check.why: A flounder lies on one side on the sea floor. If the eyes stayed on both sides, one eye would look into the sand. Moving both eyes to the upper side lets her see all round while she hides.

flow.context: This is day 4 of the Symmetry Notebook. You find useful lopsidedness.

challenges.title: Badge Designer: exactly the number of symmetries you are asked for
challenges.problem: Design a round badge with exactly 3 symmetries, then one with exactly 2, then one with exactly 1. Count each design the way you did in the Fit-Back Count, with turns and flips. Then ask a friend for a number from 4 to 8 and design a badge for it.
constraints: Each badge must fit inside a circle 8 centimetres across.
Use only lines, curves, dots and colours. No letters.
The badge must have exactly the number of symmetries asked for, not more.
Test each badge by tracing it on tracing paper, then turning and flipping the paper.
materials: a katori lid or compass for drawing circles 8 centimetres across
a ruler and a protractor, if you have them
general: For exactly 1 symmetry, draw anything lopsided, such as a hand or a leaf with a bent tip.
For exactly 2 symmetries, draw a shape with one mirror line down the middle, like a kite.
For exactly 3 symmetries, draw three curved blades twisted the same way, like a fan. A mirror line would give 6, not 3.
creative: Make a badge with 2 symmetries that uses a half turn and no mirror line, like the letter S or a yin-yang symbol.
Make a badge with 4 symmetries using two mirror lines and a half turn, like a rectangle.
Make a badge with exactly 5 symmetries. Think about a fan with five twisted blades.
challenges.your_turn: Choose a number from 4 to 8. Design a badge with exactly that number of symmetries. Test it by tracing and turning. Show a friend the badge without the number, and ask them to count its symmetries.
challenges.safety: A grown-up helps with the compass point if you use one.

setup.art: A circle on paper with a badge drawn inside it, three curved blades twisted the same way, like a fan.
setup.caption: 1. Draw an 8 centimetre circle and design a badge inside it.

setup.art: A badge traced onto tracing paper and held over the original, being turned a third of a turn.
setup.caption: 2. Trace the badge. Turn the tracing and fit it back to count the turns.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Draw an 8 centimetre circle for each badge. Talk about the three badges needed first.
flow.say: We need a badge with exactly three symmetries. What shapes have three turns but no flips? Think of a fan. Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: Draw some ideas for a badge with exactly three symmetries.

ask.q: What kind of shape has turns but no flips?
good: A fan with twisted blades.
A pinwheel.
A shape that looks different in a mirror.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Badge Designer challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Draw a badge with exactly 3 symmetries. Draw one with exactly 2. Draw one with exactly 1.
flow.say: Draw your first badge, the one with exactly three symmetries. Then try the two-symmetry badge and the one-symmetry badge.
flow.kid: Draw three badges. One has 3 symmetries. One has 2. One has 1.
flow.parent: For exactly 3, the blades must twist. If a child draws three plain straight petals, the badge has 6. Ask them to twist each blade the same way.
flow.context: In this step, you draw the first three badges.

flow.do: Test each badge. Trace it on tracing paper. Turn the tracing and fit it back. Count the fits. Then flip the tracing and count again. Fix any badge that does not have the right count.
flow.say: Trace the badge. Turn the tracing and see how many turns fit. Then flip it and count the flips. Is the count what you wanted?
flow.kid: Trace each badge. Turn it. Flip it. Count the fits.

check.q: A badge looks the same after a third of a turn, but a flip changes it. How many symmetries does it have?
check.why: The third turns are 3 symmetries, counting the do-nothing move. A flip changes the badge, so there are no flip symmetries to add. A badge with mirror lines as well would have 6.

flow.context: In this step, you test your badges by tracing, turning and flipping.

flow.do: Make a badge for a number from 4 to 8 chosen by a friend. Show it to them without the number and ask them to count the symmetries.
flow.say: Choose a number from four to eight for a friend. Make a badge with that many symmetries. Can they count the symmetries and find the number?
flow.kid: Make a badge for a number you are given. Can a friend count its symmetries?

ask.q: What makes a number of symmetries easy or hard to make?
good: A number like 6 is easy. A flower with 3 petals and 3 mirror lines gives 6.
A number like 5 or 7 needs a fan with that many twisted blades, because mirror lines would double the count.

flow.context: In this step, you design a badge for a number chosen by a friend.

items.p: Which of these is NOT one of the four moves that can leave a pattern looking the same?
items.why: The four moves are the slide, the flip, the turn and the glide. A stretch changes the size of a shape, so the shape no longer looks the same.

items.p: A move that flips a shape and slides it along at the same time is called a ____.
items.why: A glide is a flip and a slide together. Footprints along a path, with the left and right foot alternating, follow a glide.

items.p: A rectangle that is not a square is traced and cut out. In how many ways does it fit back into its outline?
items.why: It fits with no turn, a half turn, and two flips along its two middle lines. That is 4. A quarter turn does not fit, because the sides are different lengths.

items.p: A shape with no line of symmetry can still fit back into its outline by turning.
items.why: True. The letter S has no fold line, but it fits back after a half turn. A pinwheel with twisted blades fits after a turn but not after a flip.

items.p: Which of these shapes fits back into its outline in the most ways?
opts: A triangle with three equal sides
A rectangle that is not a square
items.why: A circle fits back after any turn, and after a flip across any line through its centre. That is endless. The square has 8, the equal-sided triangle 6 and the rectangle 4.

items.p: Sort each thing by whether its mirror twin can be turned to match it.
cats: Handed (the mirror twin does not fit by turning)
Not handed (it matches its mirror twin)
items: Handed (the mirror twin does not fit by turning)
Not handed (it matches its mirror twin)
Handed (the mirror twin does not fit by turning)
Not handed (it matches its mirror twin)
Handed (the mirror twin does not fit by turning)
Not handed (it matches its mirror twin)
items.why: A handed thing has no mirror line, so its mirror twin is a different thing. A shoe, a screw and scissors are handed. A katori, a round plate and the letter H match their mirror twins.

items.p: Put the steps of the Fit-Back Count in order.
items: Fit the shape back into its outline and read the letters from the star
Turn and flip the shape until no new letter pattern appears
Trace each shape and put a star on the outline
Write letters at the corners on both sides
a: Write letters at the corners on both sides
Trace each shape and put a star on the outline
Fit the shape back into its outline and read the letters from the star
Turn and flip the shape until no new letter pattern appears
items.why: First make the shapes, then label both sides so you can tell a flip from a turn, then trace and mark a start. Only then can you read the letters and keep turning and flipping until nothing new appears.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: The same shape moved along without turning
A mirror image across a line
Rotating a shape around a centre
A flip and a slide done together
Its mirror twin cannot be turned to match it
items.why: These five words are the vocabulary of symmetry. A strong answer could give an example of each: mangoes along a border for a slide, a butterfly for a flip, a fan for a turn, footprints for a glide and a hand for handed.

items.p: How many different kinds of border pattern are there?
items.why: Mathematicians have proved there are exactly 7 kinds of border pattern, however clever the design. There are 17 kinds for covering a floor.

items.p: A regular shape with 9 equal sides fits back into its outline in ____ ways.
items.why: A regular shape with n sides has n turns and n flips. For 9 sides, 9 plus 9 is 18.

items.p: Two mirrors are hinged at 60 degrees with an object between them. How many objects do you see in all, including the real one?
items.why: 360 divided by 60 is 6. The real object and its copies make 6 objects in all, arranged round the hinge.

items.p: In the pushed strip test, the push was the same at both ends. Explain what decided which way the strip bent.
items.a: A tiny hidden curve in the strip decided. An even push has no side to favour, so something small and uneven, such as a slight curl in the card, made the strip go one way. When the strip was turned over, the bend turned over with it.
items.why: A strong answer says the push was even, names a tiny difference as the decider, and uses the evidence of the curled strips or the turned-over strip.

items.p: Draw a badge that has exactly 2 symmetries and no mirror line. Say what it is.
items.a: For example the letter S or a yin-yang symbol, which fit back after the do-nothing move and a half turn only.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a shape that matches itself after a half turn but not after a flip, such as a pair of curved blades pointing opposite ways.

items.p: Label the drawing of a square: draw one line of symmetry and write how many symmetries the square has in all.
items.a: A dotted line through the middle of two opposite sides or through two opposite corners, and the number 8.
items.why: A square has 4 turns and 4 flips, which makes 8. The 4 flips are across 4 lines: two through the middle of opposite sides and two corner to corner.
items.art: A large drawing of a square with the four corners marked.

items.p: A left glove will never fit your right hand, however you turn it. Why?
opts: The glove and your right hand are mirror twins, and no turning changes a thing into its mirror twin
items.why: A left glove is the mirror twin of a right glove. Turning only moves a thing round in space and cannot reverse its handedness. To change it, you need a flip, which is not possible for a real glove.

items.p: Three of these are handed. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Scissors, a screw and a chappal each have a mirror twin that does not fit by turning. A round steel plate matches its mirror image, so it is not handed.

items.p: A regular shape fits back into its outline in 20 ways. How many equal sides does it have?
items.why: The number of ways is double the number of sides, because a regular shape has as many flips as turns. 20 divided by 2 is 10.

items.p: A badge looks the same after a quarter turn, a half turn and a three-quarter turn, but any flip changes it. How many symmetries does it have?
items.why: The badge fits back after no turn, a quarter turn, a half turn and a three-quarter turn. That is 4. The flips do not work, so none are added.

items.p: Because the push is the same at both ends, a card strip will bend towards each side equally often, even if one strip has a tiny curl.
items.why: False. A strip with a tiny curl bends the way its curl favours almost every time. The even push leaves the choice open, and the tiny difference makes it.

items.p: A cobalt experiment in 1957 counted electrons thrown out in two directions. More came out one way. What does this show?
opts: The weak force behaves differently in a mirror world
All forces are the same in a mirror
Cobalt atoms are handed like gloves
items.why: If the weak force were the same in a mirror, equal numbers would come out both ways. Because the counts differed, a mirror version of the experiment would give a different result.

items.p: If the laws of nature do not change with time, Emmy Noether proved that ____ is never used up.
items.why: Laws that do not change from one day to the next go with conservation of energy. Energy can move and change form, but the total stays the same.

items.p: The proteins in living bodies are built from ____-handed amino acids.
items.why: Life uses left-handed amino acids almost everywhere. Chemists can make both hands, but living bodies use mostly one. Nobody knows why.

items.p: Sort each body part by whether an even or a lopsided body helps.
items: a barn owl's ears at different heights
a male fiddler crab's one huge claw
the flounder's two eyes on one side
items.why: The owl locates sound by comparing the two ears, the crab uses one big claw for signalling, and the flounder lies on one side. Matching wings and fins help butterflies and fish move straight.

items.p: Match each example to the move that makes it.
pairs: A row of identical mangoes on a saree border
Footprints with the left and right foot alternating
items.why: A border of identical shapes is a slide. Footprints are a glide. The letter S matches itself after a half turn. A butterfly's wings match after a flip. A hand outline matches itself only if left where it is.

items.p: Mathematicians have shown there are exactly 17 kinds of repeating floor pattern. What does this tell a designer?
opts: Every repeating floor pattern is one of 17 kinds, however new it looks
Only 17 floor designs can be drawn
Nobody can invent a new floor design
items.why: The 17 kinds describe the way a pattern repeats, not the pictures in it. There are endless pictures, but each repeating floor still repeats in one of 17 ways.

items.p: A scientist who sees a result that every textbook says is impossible should throw the result away.
items.why: False. A surprising result should be checked, repeated and tested by others. Dan Shechtman's five-fold pattern looked impossible, but it held up and won a Nobel Prize in 2011.

items.p: Put these shapes in order, from the fewest to the most ways of fitting back into their outline.
items: A triangle with three different sides
A rectangle that is not a square
a: A triangle with three different sides
A rectangle that is not a square
items.why: The triangle with three different sides fits in 1 way. The rectangle fits in 4, the square in 8 and the hexagon in 12.

items.p: Many viruses build their shell from copies of one small piece. Why does this mean the virus needs fewer instructions than if every piece were different?
items.a: The virus only has to carry the instructions for one piece. The copies of the piece then join together by themselves, and the shell ends up with symmetry. A shell of many different pieces would need instructions for every piece.
items.why: A strong answer connects repeating a piece with saving instructions, and says that symmetry is a result of building from identical copies.

items.p: A friend says, 'A mirror swaps left and right.' Give one reason this seems true and one reason to doubt it.
items.a: It seems true because your right hand looks like a left hand in the mirror. It can be doubted because the mirror only swaps front and back. The left-right swap comes from how you imagine turning round to stand where your reflection stands.
items.why: A strong answer gives both sides. A mirror reverses the direction that points towards it, not left and right.

items.p: Draw a border made of three copies of the letter F using a glide. Mark the line each F is flipped across.
items.a: An upright F, then an upside-down mirror F slid along, then an upright F slid further along, with a dotted line running along the middle of the border.
items.why: A glide flips each F across a line along the border and slides it to the next place. A strong drawing alternates upright and upside-down Fs, each one further along.

items.p: Label the drawing of the two hinged mirrors: mark the hinge, mark the angle, and write how many objects you see in all if the angle is 90 degrees.
items.a: An arrow to the corner where the mirrors meet for the hinge, an arc inside it for the angle, and the number 4.
items.why: The hinge is where the mirrors meet. At 90 degrees, 360 divided by 90 is 4, so you see 4 objects in all.
items.art: Two hinged mirrors seen from above standing open at a right angle with a small object between them.

items.p: Two friends test a flattened card strip and it bends the same way 9 times out of 10.

views.says: The strip bent that way because my left hand pushes harder than my right hand.
The strip bent that way because the card has a tiny hidden curve that favours one side.

items.ask: Which friend do you agree with more? Say what test could show who is right.
items.a: A strong answer says how to test: turn the strip over. If the bend turns over with the strip, the strip's curve decides. If the bend stays the same, the hands may decide. Either friend could be right, and the test settles it.
items.why: The turned-over test separates the two explanations. A strong answer proposes a test, and does not just pick a friend.

items.p: A baby flounder swims upright with an eye on each side. Later one eye moves to the other side of the head. What does this show?
opts: A body can begin even and become lopsided as it grows
All fish eventually have both eyes on one side
Eyes are the only lopsided part of the body
items.why: The baby starts out even and the adult is lopsided in a useful way. This is a body breaking its own symmetry as it grows, not a mistake.

items.p: Which of these shapes has exactly 5 symmetries?
opts: A five-bladed pinwheel with blades all twisted the same way
items.why: The pinwheel fits back after 5 turns and no flip works. A regular pentagon and a five-pointed star have 5 turns and 5 flips, which makes 10. A circle has endless.

items.p: A badge fits back in 9 ways and has no flips. How many equal turns does it have?
items.why: With no flips, every symmetry is a turn. So the badge has 9 equal turns, counting the do-nothing move.

items.p: A shape with two mirror lines at right angles must also fit back after a half turn.
items.why: True. Flipping across one line and then across the other line gives a half turn. A rectangle shows it: two flips make a half turn.

items.p: A flat shape that looks reversed when you see it from behind has no line of ____.
items.why: If a shape has a line of symmetry, its back view looks just the same as the front. If it looks reversed from the back, no fold line matches its halves.

items.p: Which pair of moves, done one after the other, gives a half turn?
opts: A flip across one line, then a flip across a line at right angles to it
Two slides in the same direction
A flip across a line, then a slide
items.why: Two flips across lines that cross at a right angle make a half turn about the point where the lines cross. You can check it with a cut-out F.

items.p: A shape is flipped across a line, then flipped across the same line again. What is the result?
items.why: The first flip swaps the two sides of the line. The second flip swaps them back, so the shape is exactly where it started.

items.p: Cut out an F. Draw two lines that cross at a point on paper. Flip the F across the first line, then flip the result across the second line. Describe what happened.
items.a: The F ends up turned round the crossing point, not flipped. Two flips make a turn. The angle of the turn is double the angle between the two lines.
items.why: A strong answer says that two flips make a turn and notices that the F is no longer a mirror image after two flips.

items.p: In the pushed strip test, a tiny difference decided the direction. Give one more example from daily life where a tiny difference decides a big result, and say what the even start was.
items.a: For example a coin standing on its edge falls heads or tails. The even start is the coin balanced on its edge, and a tiny draught or a speck of dust decides the result.
items.why: A strong answer names an even start and a tiny difference that tips it. A pencil on its tip, a ball on top of a dome and a rolling die all work.

items.p: Scientists argue about why life uses left-handed amino acids.

views.says: It was chance. A tiny excess of one hand in one place got copied until life used only that hand.
The weak force treats left and right differently, so it may have nudged molecules towards one hand.

items.ask: Which explanation do you find more convincing? What evidence would you want to see?
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, and then says what evidence would help: a measurement that the nudge from the weak force is big enough to matter, or a way to see whether chance would give the same hand on another world.
items.why: The question is open. A strong answer separates what is known from what is guessed and asks for evidence.

items.p: A scientist says, 'Life uses left-handed amino acids because the weak force pushed molecules that way.' What would you most want to see before believing it?
opts: A measurement showing that the push is big enough to matter
A famous person repeating the claim
A beautiful picture of the molecules
items.why: The weak force does treat left and right differently, but the effect on molecules is extremely small. A strong claim needs a measurement showing the effect is big enough.

items.p: Sort each of these by whether it is its own mirror twin.
items.why: The letter T and a round dosa have mirror lines, so they match their own mirror images. The letter R, a spiral staircase and a corkscrew wind or lean one way, so their mirror twins are different things.

items.p: Match each idea to an example.
pairs: A pencil on its tip falling in one direction
Energy that moves and changes form but is never lost
An orderly pattern that never repeats
A shape whose mirror twin cannot be turned to match it
items.why: Each word names a different idea. A strong answer could give a second example of each, such as a straw buckling for symmetry breaking.

items.p: Draw one pattern with a half turn symmetry and no mirror line. Draw another pattern with a mirror line and no half turn.
items.a: For example the letter S for the first, and an isosceles triangle or a leaf shape for the second.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a dotted line on the second pattern and an arrow showing the half turn on the first. The two patterns show that turning and flipping are different kinds of symmetry.

items.p: The thinker Anaximander is reported to have said the Earth stays still because it is equally far from everything, so it has no reason to move one way rather than another. Using what you found with the pushed strip, say what is missing from his argument.
items.a: In the strip test, equal pushes still gave a bend, because a tiny difference made one side win. A perfectly even situation can still end up lopsided, so an argument that there is no reason to move may not show that nothing moves.
items.why: A strong answer uses the strip test as evidence: an even situation can still be tipped by a tiny difference, so 'no reason to move' is not the same as 'will not move'.

items.p: You raise your right hand in front of a mirror and your reflection seems to raise its left hand. Which direction does a flat mirror really reverse?
items.why: Your nose points towards the mirror and the nose in the mirror points back at you, so front and back are swapped. Left and right only seem swapped because you imagine turning round to stand where your reflection stands.

quiz.p: Which move flips a shape over a line, like looking in a mirror?
quiz.why: A reflection is a flip over a line. A translation is a slide and a rotation is a turn. Stretching changes the size, so it is not a symmetry.

quiz.p: A saree border shows the same mango again and again, all pointing the same way, with each one further along. Which move makes this border?
quiz.why: When every copy faces the same way and each is moved along the border, the move is a slide. A flip or a half turn would make some copies face the other way.

quiz.p: A regular octagon, with 8 equal sides, fits back into its outline in how many ways?
quiz.why: A regular shape has as many flips as turns. For 8 sides, 8 turns plus 8 flips is 16. The answer 8 forgets the flips.

quiz.p: Which of these fits back into its outline in only one way?
opts: A triangle with three equal sides
quiz.why: A hand has no turn and no flip that fits, so only the do-nothing move works. The square has 8 ways, the equal-sided triangle 6 and the rectangle 4.

quiz.p: A border has an F, then an upside-down mirror F slid along, then an F, then an upside-down mirror F, and so on. Which move made it?
quiz.why: Each new F is a flip over a line along the border and a slide, done together. That is a glide.

quiz.p: Which of these has a mirror twin that cannot be turned to match it?
quiz.why: Scissors have a handedness. The left-handed pair is the mirror twin of the right-handed pair, and no turning makes one into the other. A thali, a ball and a square tile match their mirror images.

quiz.p: A tall pencil balanced on its tip falls over, though nobody pushes it. What is the best description of what happened?
opts: An even start ended lopsided, and a tiny difference decided the direction
The pencil chose where to fall
quiz.why: Before the fall, every direction was equally likely. A tiny draught, a speck or a wobble in the wood decided the direction. Scientists call this symmetry breaking.

quiz.p: A card strip is pushed equally from both ends and bows to the same side 10 times out of 10. What does this most likely mean?
opts: The strip has a hidden tiny curve that favours that side
The push was perfectly even and strips always do this
quiz.why: An even push leaves both sides open, so something small must favour one side. A hidden curve in the card fits best. You can test it by turning the strip over.

quiz.p: Why might a barn owl benefit from having her ears at different heights?
opts: She can tell how high a sound is from the small difference in when it reaches each ear
It is only an accident of growing
quiz.why: A sound from above reaches one ear a tiny moment before the other. The owl uses the difference to find a mouse she cannot see. A lopsided part can be an advantage.

quiz.p: Most people have the heart on the left although the body looks even outside. What do scientists think helps start this difference?
opts: Tiny spinning hairs in the early embryo sweep fluid to one side
quiz.why: In mouse embryos, tiny hairs called cilia spin and sweep fluid to one side, which starts a chain of signals. Scientists think humans work in a similar way, but they are still studying it.

quiz.p: Emmy Noether proved that a symmetry in the laws of nature goes with what?
opts: Something that stays the same, such as energy
quiz.why: Noether showed that each smooth symmetry of the laws, such as the laws being the same on every day, goes with something that is conserved, such as energy.

quiz.p: What did the cobalt experiment led by Chien-Shiung Wu show?
opts: The weak force is not the same in a mirror
quiz.why: More electrons came out in one direction than the other. So a mirror copy of the experiment would give a different result, and the weak force can tell left from right.
