applications: Designers use the seven border patterns and the seventeen floor patterns to plan sarees, tiles, carpets and wallpaper.
Drug makers choose the right hand of a molecule for a medicine, because the body's proteins are handed and the two hands of one medicine can act differently.
Crystal scientists use symmetry to work out where atoms sit from the pattern of spots in an X-ray picture.
Physicists use symmetry to guess the form of new laws. Noether's theorem links each symmetry to something that is conserved.
Makers of left-handed scissors, desks, guitars and can openers build the mirror twins of the usual tools.
A kaleidoscope uses two or three mirrors at an angle to make a pattern with turn symmetry.
Doctors read X-rays and scans knowing where organs should sit, so a heart on the other side is noticed at once.
Computer artists draw one small piece of a design and let the machine repeat it with slides, flips and turns.
Quasicrystals are hard and slippery, and engineers have tested them as coatings.
Engineers build aircraft, bridges and gopurams with mirror symmetry so that loads are shared evenly.

open_questions.q: Why does life use left-handed amino acids and right-handed sugars?
open_questions.why_open: Chemists can make both hands, and no one has shown how life ended up with just one. Chance, a push from the weak force and seeding from space are all being studied.

open_questions.q: How does the human embryo first choose its left side?
open_questions.why_open: Spinning cilia are shown in mouse embryos. Some animals seem to use earlier signals. How much each matters in people is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Why do most snail shells coil the same way?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found genes that decide the coiling in some snails, but no one has a settled reason why one direction is so much commoner.

open_questions.q: Are there symmetries in the laws of nature that we have not found?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists have proposed extra symmetries to explain puzzles in particle physics. None has been confirmed by an experiment.

open_questions.q: Why do people find symmetrical patterns pleasing?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies suggest that symmetrical shapes are easier for the eye to take in. Others find the link to beauty weak or different between cultures.

open_questions.q: Are there quasicrystals in places we have not looked?
open_questions.why_open: Natural quasicrystals were found in a meteorite, and scientists are looking for how they formed and where else they may be.

maths.problem: A regular shape has 12 equal sides. How many ways does it fit back into its outline? How many more ways is that than a square, which fits in 8 ways?
maths.answer: 24 ways, which is 16 more than the square.
maths.explain: A regular shape with n sides has n turns and n flips, so 2 times n ways. 2 times 12 is 24. The square fits in 8 ways, and 24 take away 8 is 16.
maths.context: In the Fit-Back Count, you found how many ways shapes fit back into their outlines, and saw a pattern with the number of sides.
maths.why_maths: The pattern of doubling lets you predict the count for a shape you have not cut out.

maths.problem: A shape with equal sides fits back into its outline in 30 ways. How many sides does it have? How do you know?
maths.explain: The number of ways is 2 times the number of sides, so the number of sides is half of 30. 30 divided by 2 is 15.
maths.context: In the Fit-Back Count, a shape with n equal sides fits back in 2 times n ways.
maths.why_maths: Working the rule backwards tells you the shape from its count, which is how a scientist might identify a pattern.

maths.problem: Two mirrors are hinged at 36 degrees with an object between them. How many objects do you see in all, including the real one?
maths.explain: The number of objects is 360 divided by the angle. 360 divided by 36 is 10.
maths.context: In the Two Mirrors activity, you hinged two mirrors and counted the objects you saw at different angles.
maths.why_maths: The full turn is 360 degrees. Splitting it into equal angles tells you how many copies fit round the hinge.

maths.problem: A friend wants to see exactly 9 objects in all in the two mirrors. What angle should the mirrors make? What about 7 objects?
maths.answer: 40 degrees for 9 objects. For 7 objects the angle is about 51.4 degrees, which is not a whole number of degrees.
maths.explain: The angle is 360 divided by the number of objects. 360 divided by 9 is 40. 360 divided by 7 is about 51.4. It still works, but it is hard to set exactly with a protractor. Whole-number angles come from numbers that divide 360 exactly, such as 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 12.
maths.context: In the Two Mirrors activity, the number of objects was 360 divided by the angle.
maths.why_maths: Dividing 360 by the number of copies you want gives the angle, and factors show which angles are easy to set.

maths.problem: Tara pushed strip A ten times. It bent towards her 7 times and away 3 times. Strip C bent away 10 times. What fraction of strip A's tries bent towards her? What percentage is that?
maths.explain: The fraction is 7 over 10. As a percentage, 7 tenths is 70 per hundred, so 70 percent. Strip C is 0 towards and 10 away, so 100 percent away.
maths.context: In the Pushed Strip test, you tallied how many times each strip bent towards you and away from you.
maths.why_maths: A fraction or a percentage turns a tally into a number you can compare between strips.

maths.problem: Maha tossed a fair coin 10 times and got 7 heads. Does this show the coin is unfair? How could she find out?
maths.answer: No, not by itself. 7 heads in 10 tosses is quite common with a fair coin. She could toss it 100 times and see whether the heads stay near half.
maths.explain: A fair coin often gives 6, 7 or 4 heads in 10 tosses. A small number of tries is too few to be sure. With 100 tosses, a fair coin gives heads close to 50 times. The same applies to the strip: 7 out of 10 could be chance, but 10 out of 10 on many tries is not.
maths.context: In the Pushed Strip test, strip A bent the same way many times out of 10, and you ask whether that was chance.
maths.why_maths: Knowing how much chance can vary tells you when a result is strong enough to trust.

maths.problem: Each F in a border takes 6 centimetres along the strip, and the first F starts at 0. The strip is 40 centimetres long. How many whole Fs start on the strip?
maths.explain: The Fs start at 0, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and 36 centimetres. The next would start at 42, which is past the end. 40 divided by 6 is 6 with a remainder of 4, and the first F at 0 makes it 7.
maths.context: In the Stamp a Border activity, you slid an F stencil along a strip of paper in equal steps.
maths.why_maths: Division with a remainder tells you how many repeats fit, which designers need for a border.

maths.problem: A curvy tile started as a square, 6 centimetres on each side. A page is 24 centimetres by 18 centimetres. How many tiles cover the page, and why is the area of the curvy tile still 36 square centimetres?
maths.answer: 12 tiles. The curvy tile has the same area as the square because the piece cut away was added back, so nothing was lost or gained.
maths.explain: 24 divided by 6 is 4 tiles across, and 18 divided by 6 is 3 tiles down. 4 times 3 is 12. The area of the square is 6 times 6, which is 36 square centimetres. Sliding a piece from one side to the other does not change the total area.
maths.context: In the A Tile That Tiles activity, you slid a piece from one side of a square to the opposite side and covered a page.
maths.why_maths: Area stays the same when you move a piece, which is why the curvy tile still covers the page with no gaps.

how_we_found_out.story: For decades, almost every physicist believed that no law of nature could tell left from right. If you filmed any experiment in a mirror, they thought, the mirror film would obey the same laws. This was true for gravity, electricity and magnetism. In 1956, two theorists, Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang, noticed that nobody had ever tested it for the weak force, the force behind some kinds of radioactive decay. They needed an experimenter. Chien-Shiung Wu, working with a team at the United States National Bureau of Standards, cooled radioactive cobalt almost to absolute zero inside a magnet, so its atoms lined up. Then the team counted the electrons thrown out in each direction. More came out one way than the other. A mirror film of the experiment would show the opposite, so the mirror world was not the same as ours. The result was published in 1957. Lee and Yang received the Nobel Prize that year. Wu was not included.
how_we_found_out.who: Chien-Shiung Wu, an experimental physicist (1912 to 1997), with Ernest Ambler and colleagues, testing an idea of Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen-Ning Yang
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Physicists believed that every law of nature looks the same in a mirror. Wu's experiment showed that the weak force does not.
